220. To provide for the Canadian Forces, the defence research board and other expenditures relating to defence, including costs incurred in the participation of the Canadian forces in the United Nations emergency force and contributions toward the military costs of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; to authorize expenditures in the current year out of the amount hereby provided, not exceeding $130,000,000, under the provisions of section 3 of the Defence Appropriation Act, 1950, and to provide that, notwithstanding subsection (3) of that section, where equipment or supplies are transferred, the estimated present value thereof shall be credited to this vote instead of being paid into the special account mentioned in the said subsection (3), and when so credited may be expended for the purposes of the Canadian forces; and notwithstanding section 30 of the Financial Administration Act to authorize total commitments for the foregoing purposes of $3,158,845,866 regardless of the year in which such commitments will come in course of payment (of which it is estimated that $1,350,597,670 will come due for payment in future years), $1,630,377,196.

The estimates of my department which are now before this committee, Mr. Chairman, have already been examined in detail by the members of the standing committee on estimates. Of course this in no way limits the right of members of this committee to ask any questions they may wish. However, at the numerous meetings of the committee on estimates which were held during the course of the past two months, my department endeavoured to present as full a picture as possible of Canada's defence effort. The hard work performed by members of the committee deserves my thanks and appreciation. The conduct of the proceedings reflects credit on the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Calgary South. I can assure the house that a careful study will be made, both by myself and by the officials of the department, of the recommendations submitted by that committee. Many of those recommendations are most helpful, and are in line with present thought in the department.
These estimates which this committee is asked to approve were prepared a year ago, and they mark the final phase of a program which was originated to meet the conditions which existed at the time of the Korean war. You will recall that at that time the Department of National Defence increased substantially the strength of our three services, and undertook an extensive building program.

Supply-National Defence The period which began in 1950 is now coming to an end. The construction program is in the final stage, and a number of steps have been taken in connection with the reorganization of the three services.
We are now entering a new era in defence, an era when the threat of the manned bomber is being supplemented by the threat of a missile. The government will take measures to meet this new threat to our security. It is significant that during the past year attention has been focused on Canada's growing role in world affairs. In the Middle East, Canada contributes a major component to the United Nations emergency force now serving in Egypt. In this force there are over 900 Canadian army personnel and some 100 members of the R.C.A.F. The members of our armed services serving in that area deserve the highest praise for the work that they are carrying out, work which is done under extremely trying conditions.
In addition, we are taking part in the United Nations supervisory organization in Palestine, and have recently increased the number of Canadian personnel serving with the observer group in Lebanon. We are able to provide these personnel to the various United Nations missions without impairing the operational element of our services. The fact that Canada has fulfilled these requests for assistance may be an indication that in future we will be asked to accept further commitments to help maintain peace in troubled areas. If Canada should again be asked to send a force on some mission such as UNEF we have a stand-by battalion in readiness for such an eventuality.
With reference to our contribution to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization the fourth Canadian infantry brigade is presently stationed in Germany as part of the shield forces of NATO. The nuclear concept of war postulates the possibility that our major ports and lines of communication could be severely damaged in the initial enemy attack. Hence there is some doubt as to whether or not formations on this continent could reach Europe during the early and critical phase of the war. Canada, however, remains committed to furnishing the balance of an infantry division to NATO in the event of hostilities, but the portion of these forces stationed in Canada is now regarded as a strategic reserve. In order to rotate our brigade in Europe and maintain forces for the defence of Canada we have three brigade groups located respectively in the western, central and eastern areas of Canada. Each of these groups contains troops especially equipped and trained for operations in northern Canada.

In the light of new weapons developments, some major re-equipping of our army cannot long be delayed. Intensive study is now being given as to the new weapons which should be procured.
Canada's first air division with its 12 squadrons of interceptor aircraft is also in position in Europe as part of our NATO commitment, and it provides an important component of the fourth allied tactical air force under SACEUR. In addition, the Royal Canadian Navy has a number of ships earmarked for the NATO supreme allied commander, Atlantic, in the event of an emergency.
I would like to emphasize the importance of the anti-submarine role of our navy. With the advent of nuclear power and the knowledge that missiles can be fired from submarines far from our shores, our seaward defences take on increasing significance. The latest destroyer escorts now coming into service are effective weapons against the modern submarine.
In view of this changed concept of modern war at sea, there is no longer a requirement for a cruiser component in the Royal Canadian Navy. H.M.C.S. Quebec has been taken out of commission and placed in reserve at Sydney, Nova Scotia. Our other cruiser, H.M.C.S. Ontario, has been carrying out the role of training ship to the fleet. It has been decided now to decommission the Ontario and declare her and the Quebec surplus to requirements. The training functions which have been carried out by the Ontario will be transferred to an operational frigate squadron. The training received in the ships of this group will be based on the requirements of the present fleet.
Some economies will result from these changes. These include the cruiser's annual running cost amounting to $1,600,000, and the not inconsiderable cost of maintaining these ships in reserve. The officers and men now serving in the Ontario are required to man the new destroyer escorts now being completed.
One recent acquisition to our anti-submarine forces has been the Argus, a long-range patrol aircraft now coming into operational service. This aircraft, capable of sustained flight for in excess of 20 hours and armed with the latest anti-submarine weapons, increases the effectiveness of our maritime defence.
In Canada we are also making a major contribution not only to the defence of the land mass of our continent but, through our radar lines, to the alerting of the retaliatory forces of the west. It has been obvious for some time that the defence of this

continent is the joint concern of both Canada and the United States. The establishment of the joint air defence command has already received the approval of parliament, and this agreement will undoubtedly strengthen the defence of this continent. The recent announcement, following the visit of President Eisenhower to Ottawa, of a joint ministerial committee on defence will also add to mutual co-operation.
I have already referred to the high cost of new weapons. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the air. Over the years we have built up on this continent, with our United States allies, radar warning systems. It should be made clear that these systems -the DEW, the mid-Canada and the Pine-tree lines-were constructed to give warning of manned bombers. They were not meant to deal with the intercontinental ballistic missile and are not capable of so doing, but they are effective against the known capabilities of the present day bomber. However, steps are being taken to improve the method of processing the information received through these radar lines. Automatic systems of control and of passing information must be introduced as aircraft with increased capabilities come into operation.
With the rapid advancement in weapon development the importance of carrying on research is obvious. In these estimates this committee is asked to approve the sum of $82,525,000 for the defence research board. To give members an idea of the functions of this board I might quote what I said to the standing committee on July 8 last, as follows:
The main tasks which have been assigned to the defence research board are: Defence against the ballistic missile, particularly in the field of radio propagation in high altitudes: submarine detection and anti-submarine defence systems: operational research studies of weapons systems with emphasis on the joint air defence of North America; studies of nuclear propulsion of ships: responsibility for a large part of the Canadian contribution to the international geophysical year; research in man's ability to survive in such environments as high altitudes, great speed and extreme cold; development of communications and navigational systems; improvement in conventional weapons; development of new rocket type weapons: research in the field of atomic, bacteriological and chemical warfare; research on data processing and the ever-widening use of electronics; research on propellants and explosives and scientific advice to civil defence authorities.
I might add that research into bacteriological warfare is conducted entirely as a defensive measure against the possibility of the use of bacteriological attack by hostile forces.
Before concluding I would like to say a word about the need for a high standard of
Supply-National Defence officer in our armed services. This requirement is being met in part by graduates of our service colleges. The recent decision to grant degrees at the Royal Military College at Kingston is an indication of the recognition of the high academic standards required.
In so far as the role of the reserve forces is concerned, this subject was covered in the committee. Suffice it to say that each service has an important part to play and that the members of our reserves, whose role has changed in the light of modern warfare, are adapting themselves to their new tasks with admirable spirit. The emphasis on the forces in being and the cost of equipping such forces with modern weapons has of necessity called for firm reappraisal of the allotment of available funds, but within the limitations imposed there is a continuing requirement for our reserve forces.

Mr. Chairman, the introduction of the minister's estimates gives members a chance to discuss, at least on this item and in a general way, defence considerations and strategic concepts, indeed the international situation which makes it necessary for the government to bring forward defence estimates of this magnitude in the year 1958. I propose to take advantage of this opportunity to make some observations of a general character based to a large extent on the work of the committee and on the contributions made by the minister in the committee, to our knowledge of defence matters, and in this respect I have particular reference to those of us who served on the committee. I also propose to comment upon one or two things the minister has said this morning.
The minister stressed, quite rightly, that we are entering into a new era of defence, that we are now facing new defence problems -new even in the sense that they were not with us two or three years ago-and that new methods and new steps are required to meet these new problems.
Before I deal with these more general subjects, however, I would like to join the minister in paying sincere tribute, not to the work of the committee because I sat on that committee and I therefore cannot do so, but to the contribution of the chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Calgary South who presided over our work with efficiency and fairness. I think we are all most indebted to him for the way in which he conducted the work of the committee. I believe also it will be found by the house that the report of the committee will make a valuable contribution to the work of the Department of National Defence. As the minister has pointed out, the recommendations will be given careful consideration.

Supply-National Defence
As a member of the committee I was interested to note that the power given to the committee to call for persons and papers was not exercised, and that the proceedings before it were conducted, in so far as witnesses were concerned, very much in the same way as they were conducted in the defence committee two or three years ago. Various proposals were made which the minister has pointed out, in addition to many recommendations in connection with a variety of matters. Perhaps the best way in which we on this side of the house can proceed with respect to those recommendations, if we have any comments to make upon them, would be to bring forward those comments when the particular items concerned are under consideration.
One suggestion was made with which I most heartily agree, and that was that the Department of National Defence should return to the practice of previous years and produce an annual report and a white paper on defence. The minister did submit to the committee when he appeared, a very detailed, comprehensive and useful report on defence policy. Perhaps, however, it would have been more helpful to the committee and might even have made the work of the committee somewhat more effective if the kind of report which the minister produced for the benefit of the committee had been available earlier so we might have had a chance to study it in advance, in which case perhaps our questions would have been even more intelligent than they were.
We are being asked to vote a very large sum of money for defence. It is interesting to note that the minister has found, no doubt with the best will in the world, that the international situation is such that it is not possible-and I certainly do not quarrel with him on this score-to reduce our defence expenditure, and that the direction of his department and the conduct of affairs in that department and in the services has been such as to make it impossible to reduce the amounts required through the elimination of any waste or extravagance in the department itself.
The reason we are being asked to vote this amount-and it is a very large amount indeed, and a very high proportion of our total budget-is, of course, that the international situation is such that we have to pay a very high premium for defence insurance, a premium of well over a billion and a half dollars. This emphasizes once again, if emphasis is required, that when our foreign policy fails-perhaps I should say, rather, when it does not succeed, together with the foreign policies of other countries, in establishing security in the world-then our defence expenditure becomes more burdensome, 
and in that sense diplomacy is a very important part of defence. If diplomacy had succeeded better, perhaps we should not have to spend $1,600 million for this kind of defence.
We have before us at the present time a good example of the failure of diplomacy which in its turn will have its effect on the contribution which the Canadian people will have to continue to make toward defence. I am thinking now of the failure to bring about greater stability in the Middle East and solve some of the immediate and some of the more far-reaching problems there.
I think one could say in that regard that recent diplomatic developments in that area, which in turn will have their effect on defence policy and expenditures in Canada, leave one with a feeling of discouragement and almost, at times, of despair. When action was taken in Lebanon and Jordan a few weeks ago which was considered by those taking the action to be necessary, and which was taken only after invitations from the governments concerned, it seemed to some that not only would it be possible to bring that action to an end on terms which would be satisfactory to the countries concerned and remove any danger of conflict in that area, but it seemed also to some that we might be able to take advantage of this critical situation to seek the roots of the difficulty and do something about the problem which brought about this intervention in the first place. I have felt, and so I know have other hon. members, that an opportunity was given us in that regard.
To me it was a surprising opportunity when the head of the Russian state invited the United Kingdom, the United States, France, India and the secretary general of the United Nations to what he called a summit conference which he himself said would be under the auspices of the United Nations in the sense that it could report back to the security council of the United Nations. This was to be a summit conference which, from the western point of view, would have the kind of representation which could hardly be improved upon.
But we know what happened. That original invitation was not accepted in a form which would make possible the convening of this meeting, and diplomatic negotiations began which resulted in the conference becoming a public meeting of the security council. Those of us who have been at the United Nations know what such public meetings can be. When that proposal did not finally commend itself to the head of the Russian state another proposal was put forward for a special assembly of 81 nations, also to meet in public.

So instead of having a small, informal meeting which might have done something to provide a solution to these Middle East problems, and a meeting which could have reported back to the United Nations, we were left with the alternatives of a propaganda meeting of the 11 members of the security council held in public, or of an even more propagandist meeting of the 81 members of the assembly.
That is the situation we are facing now, and I suggest that the only way in which we in the west can really accomplish something in the face of the diplomatic manoeuvres that have been going on is by putting before this assembly some constructive proposals on economic and political planning in the Middle East of the kind that might possibly have been placed before a smaller meeting. Unless we can use the assembly for that purpose-and there is not going to be much time-this assembly will deteriorate into a propaganda jamboree with charges and countercharges of aggression, direct and indirect, and it will not make much of a contribution to the solution of this problem. And unless we do this we will probably find that next year our defence estimates will be just as large as, if not larger than, they were this year.
The minister pointed out in his statement and in his report to the committee that Canadian defence policy is based, as it has been for some years, on the acceptance of various obligations. The first obligation on defence policy is, of course, the defence of our own territory, but we have other obligations which also involve the defence of Canada by action outside Canada. The minister has mentioned as one of those, our obligations under the United Nations; and in dealing with these responsibilities he pointed out what Canada is doing at the present time to discharge those obligations through the Department of National Defence. He paid tribute to the work Canadian servicemen are doing in the United Nations emergency force and in other far places of the world in the interests of peace, a tribute in which I should like sincerely to join. Not only is the United Nations emergency force operating in the Middle East, but observation groups are playing a useful and indeed a valuable role in preventing trouble in various parts of the world. There are missions in Indo-China. There are Canadian observers in Pakistan, and there are now many in Lebanon. As the minister has indicated, this international activity is a concept which I think must affect Canada's defence policy in the years ahead.
What can we do on our part to make a contribution to international police activity, which if it can do nothing else might prevent
Supply-National Defence small conflicts developing into world destructive wars? There is one concept which governed our defence concept in the past which I suggest is now obsolete and should have little if anything to do with defence planning. That is the concept that we should make preparation in Canada for sending an expeditionary force overseas, as we have had to do twice in our lifetime. It does not seem to me to be realistic to contemplate that kind of contribution by which over the months and years we would be sending troops across the Atlantic to the battlefields of Europe.
Because it is an indication that the government does realize that this is pretty much out of date in the nuclear age I was glad to hear the minister say that even our NATO obligation to bring our brigade up to divisional strength in case of conflict overseas-and that is an obligation we have undertaken-is perhaps of less importance than it was, and of less importance than some of the other obligations which face us at this time. I was also very glad to hear him say that in the discharge of this new kind of obligation to contribute toward international forces-not to win a war but to prevent a war-the department had now a battalion well equipped and available on short notice as Canada's contribution to this kind of activity. I believe that is very important, especially in the light of the possibility that in the months ahead we may be asked to make that kind of contribution along with other countries.
I am inclined to repeat here what I have said in the house before and in committees of the house, that if this kind of contribution is to be made effective-the international police force and the international observer group idea-we have to make this kind of preparation for it in advance. We have to set up a kind of permanent defence organization at United Nations headquarters and the countries who are willing to make this kind of contribution, and Canada is one of them, should let the organization in New York know in advance what they will have available and ready for any particular emergency that may develop.
I believe Canada has played a highly imaginative and constructive part in this concept. Not only did we make forces available years ago at the time of the Korean crisis, but at that time we said the forces should be made available, a brigade, subject to parliamentary approval, for any United Nations action which might be required in the future, and I think that decision still holds.
I grow a little impatient when I hear the great powers say they do not want to do this kind or that of thing, or having done it, say: "We should like to get out of it; if

Supply-National Defence only the United Nations will move in and take over our responsibility we will withdraw". That is what they say in time of crisis or emergency. But when the emergency is past and we go down to the United Nations and make a proposal for the establishment of some kind of permanent machinery which might make it unnecessary for them to intervene in the future, they can find all kinds of reasons for hesitation and delay. This would be a good time, labouring as we are under the fear of this crisis, to press ahead with this kind of international force to which Canada is now pledged to make a contribution in the future along the lines of the contributions we have made in the past.
So much for our United Nations defence obligation. We have, of course, very important defence obligations-and the minister mentioned them here and in the committee- under NATO. It is not easy for someone who does not attend the NATO meetings to ascertain exactly what is NATO strategy at the present time in the face of the new developments about which the minister has told us. It was considered, and perhaps it is still basic NATO strategy, that there should be built up in Europe balanced collective forces under a NATO commander of a strength sufficient to hold the attack well away, if possible, from the Hhine and western Europe; forces that would be strong enough not only to hold the attack away but to hold it long enough to make it possible for massive retaliation, for the deterrent to go into operation.
I recall attending the NATO council meeting in Lisbon some years ago. The military chiefs at that time said that 95 divisions would be required for that basic NATO strategy. I remember, and I am sure the minister will remember, the government of that day was very strongly attacked by the C.C.F. party in connection with that report because they said we had sold out to the military, who had demanded an impossible total for defence purposes. Well, it is interesting to recall that in the space of a few years- because that Lisbon meeting was not very long ago

the objectives that are now considered required for this basic strategy have been reduced and reduced in terms of military contributions until

I do not know exactly what they are, but they have been reduced greatly. I do know that the NATO commander in chief-and I am not betraying any secret in saying this because he made a public statement about it-did request the NATO defence ministers at the last meeting to raise the number of divisions from 15 to 30 as the minimum which was required to carry out this basic concept.

But there is another concept of basic NATO defence, and I know these matters are now under consideration by NATO committees, though I do not know if the consideration is completed. The other aspect of NATO defence is that the main function and indeed the only defensive function of NATO land and air forces is to identify an aggressor. This is the trip-wire theory of defence about which the minister knows, and only a very small force is required for identification purposes. Once an enemy has been identified and the aggression as such has been identified, then the deterrent goes into operation at once and you have your massive retaliation to defend Europe by the strategic air command of the United States going into operation from its bases.
It seems to me that the weakness of this concept is that if it is assumed by the people in the NATO countries that our only defence against aggression is massive retaliation by the strategic air command of the United States with nuclear bombs, the people of those countries will not be too anxious to make the kind of sacrifice in terms of local defence which is required because they will leave it all to massive retaliation. Because of that fact-and there is some indication that this concept dominates public opinion in some European countries-and because of the consequent weakening of our conventional defence position in western Europe and elsewhere, the massive retaliation deterrent has to get stronger, and as it gets stronger and stronger you do less in a conventional way, so you get into a vicious circle which does not seem to me to be a very satisfactory basis for collective defence.
There is no doubt-and it is one of the things that is most frightening in the present situation-that we are relying now largely on the nuclear deterrent; that this deterrent is now nuclear power of which both sides- not only one side, as was the case six or seven years ago-have more than enough in the form of missiles and bombs to blow our planet to pieces, or at least to destroy those who are inhabiting it, and yet they keep on piling bombs on top of bombs. I have never been able to understand the military reasoning which requiries 100 hydrogen bombs if 50 on each side can destroy the world.
I am informed-and on good authority, because the information comes from a United States official source-that there is enough fissionable material being produced in the United States alone each year now to make 30,000 to 40,000 atom bombs of the old-fashioned type which killed 86,000 people in

Hiroshima in one explosion. I am also informed that if this fissionable material, which is still being produced, goes into the more modern, refined hydrogen bomb there is enough material for almost a million Hiroshimas. That is the foundation of power, unbelievable power, on which our nuclear deterrent rests. We rely now for peace primarily on that deterrent.
I was reading the other day a paper by a former admiral of the British navy, Admiral A. W. Buzzard. He was chief of naval intelligence; perhaps the minister knows him. He was making a very strong attack against this reliance for our security, this sole reliance, or at least reliance to too great an extent, on this policy of massive retaliation through the nuclear deterrent. He had this to say in this paper, and perhaps the committee will forgive me if I put it on record:
This policy of massive retaliation was adopted by NATO as an emergency measure eight years ago, at the time of Korea, when we suddenly realized that we were faced by an aggressive and heavily armed communist empire, and had nothing but America's atomic bomb with which to defend ourselves. It seemed an acceptable policy to most people at the time, because the atomic bomb was then virtually an American monopoly, the Russians having very few of them and no aircraft-let alone ballistic missiles-which could reach America in retaliation.
How that situation has changed.
But now that Russia, too, has an effective nuclear deterrent-grown to megaton proportions- and she can deliver it into the heart of America, the situation is very different. For whatever we may say, the communists must increasingly doubt-
I suggest that the present situation in the Middle East is a very good illustration of this worry.
-whether America would in fact commit suicide for a serious local threat in, say, northern Scandinavia, Greece, Yugoslavia, the Middle East, southeast Asia or Korea. Thus, our nuclear deterrent, greatly increased in its severity, has been greatly decreased in its certainty of application, and the "all or nothing'' school often forgets that a deterrent, to be effective, must be reasonably certain of being applied, as well as being severe in its consequences. Indeed, it is better for it to be only reasonably severe and certain to be applied, than for it to be disastrous in its severity and uncertain of being applied.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, that is a position which does not inspire a feeling of comfort or security in anyone who contemplates our defence strategy at the present time, when we are relying to such an extent on a nuclear deterrent of such power that we cannot be sure it will be applied because the consequences of the application, or which if applied to meet local and limited aggression, would convert a local limited aggression into world war III, which would end the world.
Supply-National Defence
Because of that dilemma-and it certainly is a dilemma-we may well now find that we are not facing this kind of aggression which is going to bring about this kind of retaliation. The potential enemy, knowing perhaps that an Anglo-Saxon power will hesitate before it drops a nuclear bomb which will convert a limited aggression into world war III, knowing our hesitation in that regard, may concentrate more on direct aggression in a limited way on the periphery of the Soviet empire, or in indirect aggression, economic and political, in a big way.
That means, if it means anything at all in our defence policy, that now not only do we have to maintain a nuclear deterrent, because we have to do that, but we in the western world also have to develop enough tactical defence strength to meet this kind of aggression in various parts of the world without relying on the kind of nuclear weapons I have been talking about. That makes the task of defence policy-defence policy, of course, for the big powers, but also defence policy for all powers-a dual task; to participate in the nuclear deterrent, as Canada is in one sense, and participate also in the building up of conventional collective forces of the kind which might be required because the nuclear deterrent cannot or will not be used.
That is the second concept of defence, Mr. Chairman, the NATO concept; and the third, the one which is of most direct importance to us, is the concept of continental defence, defence of our own territory and defence of our own air, the detection and the destruction of an attack on Canada, which attack would likely be only through the air, or more likely an attack on the United States over Canada. Here is something that the minister has pointed out on more than one occasion. Here is the situation in which Canada is vitally and directly concerned and with which we cannot deal except in the closest possible association with the United States of America. That association, the importance of it and the closeness of it, has been recognized in the formation of the North American defence organization, NORAD.
I only wish-that is all I am going to say about NORAD-that this continental defence organization could be even more closely associated with NATO than the minister said it was associated now, namely in a somewhat indirect and loose way. I suggest that in respect of this aspect of defence policy, the continental aspect, there have been some vitally important changes in the situation in the last two or three years, some very important changes since the decision was made just a few years ago to construct three radar

It does raise the question whether Canada can afford this kind of participation in collective defence. This question becomes all the more urgent when we realize that when we do produce this kind of plane through the planning and designing of our own experts- it is a great credit to them and shows we have an aircraft industry in this country that can do this kind of thing as well as any industry in the world-there is practically no opportunity for operating on a continental but only on a Canadian basis.
The minister has been in Washington, and perhaps he has been trying to do something about this. I know also from my own experience in the past that when we tried to get the United States interested in the CF-100 some years ago, at a time when the CF-100 was admitted in Washington to be certainly the best all-weather fighter on this continent, we made no progress at all. The aircraft industry down there was not going to allow any interference with its own right to produce its own aircraft for its own government. I believe the minister will be having the same trouble with the CF-105.
If co-operation is to extend to the point where we integrate our air forces, then co-operation should also extend to the point where we integrate our resources. If Canadian industry can produce a weapon as good as or better than a United States weapon, then we should try to get the United States to recognize the importance of co-operation by encouraging this kind of development in Canada, not on a national but on a continental basis.
Then there is the other aspect of this question. If we are going to have the CF-105 in operation, if we are going to have the Bomarc in operation, how can we contemplate a situation where Canadian squadrons, armed if you like with the Bomarc missile-I am thinking now of the years ahead-and operating off the same air base with United States squadrons under the command of an integrated headquarters commanded by a United States commander with a Canadian deputy commander, when the Canadian squadrons would have missiles without nuclear warheads and the United States squadrons operating along with them would have nuclear warheads? It is taken for granted in the evidence I have read at congressional hearings that to be really effective to the maximum possible extent for defence purposes you should have the nuclear warheads on these particular missiles.
I do not want to be misunderstood. I am not advocating that there should be manufactured in Canada any kind of nuclear weapons, nor am I departing in any way from

the proposal I made the other day that those countries which are now manufacturing nuclear weapons for mass destruction should agree that they will not manufacture them in the future. However, that is something very different from having access to a country which does manufacture these weapons for defence purposes-I am now talking about tactical weapons-and with which we are co-operating in an integrated continental defence scheme. Under legislation passed by the United States congress these weapons cannot now be made available to a country with which it is working on continental defence. I suggest this is a situation which in the long run will not be considered tolerable in this country. I know there have been changes made in the United States atomic energy legislation during the last two or three months which deal with this matter, but it is not dealt with in a way which gives me very much satisfaction.
In these amendments the United States has singled out the United Kingdom for preferential treatment, on the ground that the United Kingdom is already in the atomic weapons business. Under the amendment to section 144 (c) of the atomic energy act, if a country can prove it has made progress in the field of manufacturing nuclear weapons it qualifies for this kind of assistance. So far as I can make out Canada does not get that kind of assistance unless it can make a separate agreement with the United States under another provision of this act.
I should like to ask the minister, when he replies in this general debate, exactly what the situation is in regard to this matter, and whether or not steps are being taken to bring about that kind of agreement which would put Canadian defence forces and United States defence forces, operating under the same command, in exactly the same position in regard to equipment.
The other day we heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the Canadian government was not asking for this kind of agreement now. We heard him say also, and it was an important statement, that there is no question about storing nuclear warheads in Canada. Then he went on to explain that this perhaps was not necessary because a quick decision could be made in Washington-he added even perhaps too quick-which would make available these nuclear warheads in time of emergency.
If they are not stored in Canada, if we have no agreement which puts them under the control of Canadians before the emergency, and if the decision has to be taken in Washington which would result in them being moved to Canada in an emergency or moved from a United States squadron on Canadian soil

to a Canadian squadron, I suggest that is not good enough; because when an emergency of that kind occurs, if it ever does, there will not be time to make these arrangements. This question ought to be cleared up before the emergency occurs.
I come then, Mr. Chairman, to the final part of my statement. I have talked about our UN obligations, our NATO obligations and our new and more extensive obligations in regard to continental defence. The question inevitably presents itself to us, as it must present itself in an even more immediate form to the minister himself, how can Canada, with its resources and with what is needed for development in other fields in this country, do all the things in the future that may be required under these three sets of obligations? I would like to quote what the minister said before the committee on June 10:
No country, particularly a country of limited means-both financial and in manpower, can be expected to promote a balanced force of all the different services.
They can concentrate on the type of production, the type of arms . . . most adaptable to the conditions of the country.
I suggest that that is exactly the principle upon which we have to operate, and that it is the application of that principle which is going to cause the difficulty. A great p0wer-for instance, the United States of America-cannot afford to take a gamble of this kind. They have to concentrate on every possible form of defence, and there is no escaping that fact because they are a great power. They have to keep on developing and building new weapons, however quickly they may become obsolete; but surely there should be a limit to what a country like Canada does or is asked to do in this field of development for defence purposes. Surely our country should not have to keep up with every move-and these moves are being made very quickly today- in respect to methods of defence, strategic and defence planning and so on, which require the production of new types of weapons.
I am certainly not attempting to be dogmatic in this regard because I know how difficult it is to come to any conclusions, but perhaps in this kind of situation, with changes taking place so swiftly and devastating with respect to methods of attack and methods of defence, Canada may have to wait before, for instance, entering into the field of rocket and missile construction. Perhaps we will also have to adopt a system of priorities of a different kind from that which we have adopted in the past with regard to defence by confining our defence efforts, or at least devoting the major part
Supply-National Defence of our defence efforts, to matters particularly concerned with questions of immediate interest to us such as radar defence, integration of ground equipment and ground control, in order words the kind of activities which, if we do not undertake them, the United States of America will ask for permission to undertake on our behalf and on their own behalf on our territory.
It may indeed become more and more necessary for us to take over the maximum responsibility possible for defence activity and facilities on our own soil, even if that means-and this is a decision which naturally no one would make very quickly or easily -some reduction in our commitments abroad under NATO. Perhaps that would be a sound national policy without, I suggest, prejudicing in any way our obligations for international co-operation and defence.
It seems clear to me, and the minister may comment on this point when he replies, that soon the major, if not the sole, instrument of air attack will be the missile, and that this will require a complete revamping of defence strategy and defence policy. It seems to me, and I speak without any expert authority in this matter, that to counter this method of attack the manned jet interceptors will one day-perhaps a day not too far distant-be as obsolete as the old BE2C of the R.F.C. in which I learned to fly, and that these manned interceptors will be replaced, at least to a large extent, by the pilotless interceptors.
That poses a question directly to the government. Are we going to go into the production and planning of these new planes and missiles, or should we not leave the production of this kind of weapon under the concept of division of tasks in a balanced collective defence strategy to the United States and concentrate our efforts in Canada, not exclusively but mostly, to ground environmental control and early warning systems against missile attack? That will give Canada a major responsibility in continental defence; it will give her great responsibility for the construction, control and maintenance of facilities on her own soil.
These are important questions which I throw out to the minister, which he will perhaps be able to answer when he replies. I want to tell him that when I ask him these questions I know it is much easier to ask than to answer them. I also want to tell him that I appreciate the dilemma in which the government must be in relation to these questions with respect to developments in the realm of defence which may or may not take place in the future. It seems to me there are many difficulties in doing these new

Supply-National Defence tasks at the expense of the contribution to defence which has proved to be most effective from our point of view in past years and which, until these new developments take place, is still essential. I know this is a very serious dilemma and that it is inescapable.
My only suggestion is that which I have outlined; that in order to resolve this dilemma perhaps we could take a greater share of responsibility for those activities upon our own soil, even though it might mean a reduction to some extent-and I am not thinking of those United Nations, activities which are very minor in terms of expense-in some other activities outside this country. I suggest it is all the more important that we approach defence in this way, because if we do take responsibility for this kind of activity in Canada it will have very important civilian implications. It will help to develop our north country and prevent that development from being not taken over, but from falling too much into the responsibility of our friend and neighbour the United States of America. This point has been very well illustrated in a recent article by Mr. John Walker, special Washington correspondent for Southam Press, which appeared in the Hamilton Spectator under the heading, "U.S. May Soon Take Over Canadian Arctic Research and Patrol Work" and which reads as follows:
The United States government may soon be taking over a significant field of research and patrol work in the Canadian Arctic, unless the Canadian government takes a more active role in Arctic development.
The Americans will not be doing this by design, but the fact that Congress has approved a bill to authorize construction of a nuclear-powered icebreaker points up the prospects that within three years the U.S. may have such a craft in operation.
The article goes on to say that this craft will be used for Arctic work, and concludes with this paragraph:
If the Canadian government continues to keep the Labrador out of real Arctic action, and does not move actively on nuclear or other powered icebreakers, it is hard to see how Canadian military and scientific men can avoid calling upon the U.S. to do the chore, perhaps by 1961 in a brand new atomic icebreaker.
I hope, therefore, that the government will be able to reconcile these two things, the desirability of playing the right part in defence and the desirability also of playing a part which will help in our development in other fields than that of defence.
May I conclude by coming back to the point at which I began, namely that no defence policy and no defence expenditure, however massive, no weapon however modern, however powerful or however new, will really give us the kind of security we must have in this world unless we can build up alongside that policy the other kind of defence policy

which rests upon an imaginative, constructive, collective and powerful diplomacy. We may have in the western world more, more and more power; we are in fact building up more, more and more power, but so are those countries behind the iron curtain.
It is quite clear, however, that this policy alone will not save us, even though without it we may be lost. Power without wisdom will avail us little. Determination and imagination in diplomacy are as essential as what the Americans call a good defence posture. Canadian defence policy, then, and indeed defence policy for the whole western world must be based on both kinds of power-military power, and political and diplomatic power.

speechtext:
In speaking on the defence
estimates I wish to join those who have congratulated the hon. member for Calgary South on the able manner in which he handled the estimates committee. Whether this was a new type of committee I do not know, but he did handle that committee in a very able manner and is to be commended on having done so. The Minister of National Defence is also to be complimented on the manner in which both he and the witnesses he presented were able to testify to the extent requested by the members of the committee.
One of the problems about discussing national defence is that of remaining within the necessary bounds of security while obtaining information which appears always to be available through many other sources, and bearing this in mind I think the committee which considered the estimates of this department did very good work in bringing to the attention of the general public some of the problems which confront the Department of National Defence and which face all Canada in its defence procedures. However, I believe the committee might have gone a little further than it did in advising the Canadian public that though we were not able to recommend any reduction in national defence expenditures, for the simple reason that each item, taken individually, has to be justified only with regard to that particular estimate, when the situation was examined more broadly it became immediately a matter of government policy and was, therefore, not completely open to question. Thus, although the items in the estimates were not related to each other they were, I think, well discussed individually, and in this respect the committee did a good job.
I believe that a number of the committee's recommendations are worth repeating and bear some relationship to what our new military policy must be. One of the recommendations which interested me concerned the question of integration. It seems that for

a long time there has been competition among the various services, though perhaps not to so great an extent as in some countries close by. But we have had competition among the various services, not only for recruits but with regard to the type of contribution each service could make. There has been a certain rivalry among the army, the navy and the air force; and while in some cases it has been good rivalry it has in others led to inefficiency. I understand that the recommendations of the committee with respect to this matter of integration are to receive consideration, particularly with regard to auxiliary services.
Another matter which in my opinion will bear a great deal more scrutiny than the committee was able to devote to it is the question of the relationship between the civil service on the one hand and military personnel on the other. It has been said that it takes two civil servants to keep every military man in the field. I am not sure that that relationship has been maintained or that it was a good one in the first place, and I question the statement that has been made on a number of occasions that it costs more to keep military personnel in the field than it does to support civilians.
This is open to question, but it was pointed out to the committee that military personnel were established on a quota basis, in other words that a certain fixed number of people were allotted to the army, the navy and the air force, a number which could not be exceeded. The tendency, therefore, would be to increase the number of civil servants whose establishment was not affected by such a restriction. I think further consideration should be given to this question, because I do not think it was proven to the committee that it is more advantageous to employ people who are in permanent positions as civil servants as against military personnel who can be retrained, reclassified and transferred if necessary in the interests of the nation.
Now this department is asking for $1,168 million, which is a very large sum of money; and when the committee-and it was a large and conscientious committee-examined each item of these estimates it was not able to recommend any reduction in this amount. I think the committee should have gone a little further than it did in considering policy and discussing how the various components which made up the estimates as a whole would fit into the over-all policy.
There has been a great change in our thinking as far as military defence is concerned. In the last few years we have discarded the old concept of using an army with auxiliary services classed as the navy 57071-3-201
Supply-National Defence and the air force. The advent of sputnik and the intercontinental missile have made necessary a complete change in our thinking on defence, and we are now faced in Canada with a great many problems with which we were not faced before.
I think it was for this reason that the committee did include in its report a statement that expenditure on defence was not likely to decrease, but rather that we could expect such expenditures to rise rapidly if the developments now contemplated are to take place within the next few years. I think this is borne out by many of the things the Leader of the Opposition said so capably today. If we are to change our concept of military defence and at the same time maintain some of our more traditional defence measures, there will be a need for a great deal more expenditure on defence.
Before I leave this subject I should like to mention that I personally, and I think the country as a whole, was very disappointed that General Simonds was not called before the committee; and while I agree that it would have meant discussing questions of government policy which might not have been within the purview of the committee, the Canadian people might well have realized some advantage from the knowledge and experience which General Simonds has acquired over the years.
Had General Simonds appeared he might well have been able to give the committee an insight into the developments which are likely to take place within the next few years, in the light of his experience and the information available to him. The other side of the argument could have been capably advanced by Air Marshal Collins and also our own Minister of National Defence. The result would not have been merely a rehashing of many ideas that have been newspaper copy for many months, but we would probably have arrived at a clearer picture of what steps must be taken with this type of consideration.
We in Canada are faced with the problem of a defence system that is now completely out of date. The radar chains are generally considered to be not sufficient for present day needs. We are developing and installing many new units that are going to be advantageous, but these are costing a great deal of money and are difficult for us to finance. The British scientists are developing a microwave amplifier called Naser which will track planes 1,000 miles away. According to my information this is a great deal superior to what we have at present. This is only one of many new developments

Supply-National Defence taking place which we will have to incorporate in our national defence system if we are going to be up to date.
When put into effect our radar chains perhaps were not sufficient for our needs but represented the best we had at the time and were considered adequate. They are no longer adequate and will have to be replaced. But even if we replace the radar chains with a radar device like Naser we will not be able to track things like intercontinental ballistic missiles. We shall have to enter that field which is more expensive than any we have previously contemplated.
The matter which has been discussed on a number of occasions, of integrating Canadian defence production with that of the United States, has caused a great deal of apprehension. Already official thinking suggests that integration of defence production and the United States and Canadian economies must shortly follow integration of air defences. The reasons are clearly apparent. Canada's air defence system based on the present radar screens and the subsonic CF-100 fighter is now admitted to be out of date. The present air defence system was designed some years ago to defend the country against the primary offensive weapon then available to the U.S.S.R. namely the non-jet TU-4 bombers. But much faster turbo-prop and jet planes such as the Bison, the Soviet's intercontinental jet bomber, as well as supersonic jet bombers now being developed, make this air defence system obsolescent.
This is one of the reasons why the United States government has been given permission to conduct the survey announced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the House of Commons on May 21. It is almost a foregone conclusion that this survey will result in the decisions to introduce the United States semi-automatic ground environment weapon known as Sage into Canadian air defence. This system is being installed in the United States, and it has been felt for some time that the same would have to be done in Canada if successful air defence integration of the two countries is to be achieved. Sage, an electronic computer capable of making 9,600 mathematical calculations per second, will automatize ground control operations. An integral part of the Sage system is Bomarc, a ground to air guided missile capable of being fitted with an atomic warhead. With the co-ordination of Sage and Bomarc it is considered possible to employ mass interception against a mass raid by jet bombers.
Canada is faced with a twofold problem. The Sage-Bomarc system will impose a tremendous financial burden on this country

as well as make it even more dependent on the technological and production skills of the United States. On the other hand, this system provides no defence whatsoever against intercontinental ballistic missiles. Therefore in order to prepare against manned jet bombers and at the same time prepare against attack's from I.C.B.M.'s, both the Sage-Bomarc and some other as yet undeveloped antimissile system must be developed. Canada is incapable of developing either system by herself.
There is no question about Canada's ability to manufacture a Sage computer based on the United States design. However, the drawback is that according to defence experts the cost of production of a single computer in Canada would be about double the estimated cost of $25 million in the United States. Then there is the recently developed high powered, long range radar now in production in the United States. These sets will have to be installed along Canada's side of the Pinetree defence line. Again these are too costly to manufacture in Canada and will have to be bought in the United States.
The implications for the Canadian economy are becoming increasingly apparent. It is reported that defence officials have come to the conclusion that Canadian industry will have to manufacture component parts for United States assemblies. The future pattern is clear. Canadian industry, if it is to get any share at all in the production of the new and complex equipment needed in the air defence of Canada, will have to content itself with participating as subcontractors in large United States production programs.
Canada is continually being faced with the problem of raising money for defence, and certainly the present requirement of over $1J billion is not a small amount. But these units cost $50 million each, and large numbers are necessary. Canada finds itself subjected to participating in the program of defending the North American continent. That is one of the reasons why we in this group opposed the entry of Canada into the NORAD agreement.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it one o'clock?

Mr. Chairman, before lunch we were drawing attention to the fact that the committee had stated that the expenditures had become increasingly large over a period of years, and the tendency appears

to be continuing. If we follow the same line of reasoning that we have followed in the past the economic burden is going to put us closely in the shadow of the United States. It is precisely because of this seemingly inevitable tie-up with the United States on the economic level that it is of great importance to avoid putting ourselves in a politically subordinate position to the United States.
While we cannot avoid becoming more and more dependent on the United States if we are to meet our air defence requirements, we can avoid making it bilateral. It is one thing to surrender sovereign rights in a multilateral treaty to such a body as NATO or the United Nations; it is an entirely different matter to surrender sovereignty to a single country in a bilateral agreement. In the case of Canada it is the latter which is accomplished in the exchange of notes affecting a form of integration of the air defences of North America. It would seem imperative from the point of view of the loss of Canada's political sovereignty to a single nation that ways and means be found to make the North American defence organization directly responsible and subordinate to the NATO command. This point of view has been ably set out in Le Devoir, which comments as follows:
Canada, as a member of NATO, shares In the defence of western Europe. Would It not be wiser and more logical to place the defence of our tremendous territory in the north in the framework of the Atlantic pact? It probably brings us into a position equal to that we reached by building the Mosquito bomber at the end of the last war.
Relatively speaking this plane compares favourably with, if it is not better than, any other plane of its type in the world; but I wonder whether the Canadian people can afford this type of luxury. While it is true we have developed the CF-105 at a cost of something over $200 million, the total program which is already blocked out will cost something over $1 billion. I am wondering whether the Canadian people are in the position of being able to enjoy the luxury that they appear to have effected for themselves in the building, the designing and the development of this particular type of aircraft.
I agree with the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition this morning when he said the committee also endorsed the idea that there should be no expansion program of this type ever undertaken by the Canadian people again without consultation with, and without getting orders from and the approval of, other countries interested in this particular field, and particularly the NATO countries. I think the CF-105 points out as well as anything does the position that Canada is going to find itself in if it looks at the situation in terms of our old line thinking on defence.
There have been suggestions made in other fields which I think are going to be endorsed, such as an investigation into civil defence. I think the committee was of the opinion that civil defence should be put back into this department under the Minister of National Defence. I am not sure that he wants it there, but I think that is where it belongs. Greater reliance must be put on the role of civil defence in the case of an atomic attack. In this field the militia can be very advantageous if they are fitted into it and do not become supernumerary to the authorities who will be controlling civil defence.
Over the years the C.C.F. have advocated a decrease in the expenditures on national defence. Today we are spending very close to one-third of our income to pay for defence which is inadequate, which cannot by any stretch of the imagination protect our major

Supply-National Defence cities from attack by an enemy agent. Therefore we should look very closely at those expenditures. We suggest that greater reliance must be put on other phases of defence. In the United Nations Canada, as a middle of the road power, should take the lead and speak for disarmament. While there are many obstacles-and we have heard them all- there are many advantages in disarmament on an international scale. We could better the lot of the Canadian people much more by spending a few million dollars on aid to other countries that need aid and helping the world to bring about disarmament in a reasonable manner so that we could, as we must, reduce our expenditure on defence, which is a wasted asset no matter how we look at it.
Finally, I suggest that the minister should give very careful consideration not only to participating in bringing about disarmament but to giving leadership to the world in that regard. In the past we gave a lead in setting up an international police force, and we have been quite successful in our approach in that field. I think Canada can accomplish a great deal more by helping the world find a way to permanent peace than by developing such programs as the CF-105. If we are going to spend, let us spend in a field that will produce peace rather than war.

Mr. Chairman, if there is no more discussion on general policy perhaps I should take a minute or two to answer some of the questions that have been raised. First of all may I, without any qualification at all, express my appreciation to the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member who has just spoken for the very helpful contributions they have made to the discussion of the general problem of national defence. I could not agree more heartily with anybody than with the Leader of the Opposition when he referred to the close link that exists between defence policy and foreign policy. The two go together, and until some complete and effective system of inspection and disarmament has been worked out amongst the nations of the world we have to maintain a reasonable defence. As soon as the powers get together and decide that wars will be no more then, as one who has taken part in two wars and seen something of the disturbed conditions since, that achievement will not be welcomed more heartily by anyone than by me.
To answer some of the definite questions asked and problems raised by the Leader of the Opposition, may I say that first of all he referred to a white paper and an annual report. As I pointed out this morning, we are really finishing up a program which had been under way since 1950, and as annual reports usually are rather out of date by the time

the estimates are discussed and as there is no statutory requirement obliging us to produce an annual report, I thought it was unnecessary to go to that expense this year. Next year we will have to start to get ready for this new era of defence, and I assure the committee that we will then prepare at least a white paper which will spell out our proposals in detail.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the dilemma which exists. He pointed out the problems which have to be solved. I am not in a position today to put forward a solution to these problems. I am not quite certain on what horn of the dilemma I must rest. We have to collect more information before we make a decision which will affect the security of the country and mean the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars over many years. As I stated in the committee, before the end of the year a decision will have to be reached in respect to many of these very difficult problems. They are with me every day and pretty nearly 24 hours of every day. Solutions will be reached and will be presented to parliament in due course.
With regard to the change of emphasis in connection with the idea of expeditionary forces, as both I and the Leader of the Opposition have pointed out the situation has changed. We are not planning to send any large expeditionary forces overseas in the early days of a war. But we do believe, and I think the Leader of the Opposition agrees, in the necessity of retaining what are frequently referred to as conventional arms. I see a growing need for contributions to be made to United Nations organizations, whether on a permanent basis or whether on an ad hoc basis of sending such forces when the need arises. We have to be ready to make our contribution to the preservation of peace, perhaps in many far distant parts of the world. I have that very much in mind, and it will be mainly conventional arms which will make that contribution.
But we do not have to maintain all the conventional arms as of old and, as I indicated last year, we have discontinued divisional headquarters and many of what are termed the divisional troops of the last war are not being maintained by Canada. I indicated in my remarks this morning, and I think this shows how we are progressing and not trying to maintain old establishments, that we have decided to decommission two cruisers. In the past these cruisers played a very important role in the defence of Canada, but conditions have changed and we are now going to declare these two grand vessels, which rendered great service to Canada in the past, surplus to our modern requirements.

Mention was made of the Bomarc. I should like to point out that the Bomarc is not in operation yet. If we wanted to get a Bomarc today we could not get one. Hon. members will have noticed in yesterday's paper that reference was made to what I think is the first experiment linking the Bomarc with a firing by remote control of one of these missiles now in the course of development. We are watching the development of this missile with great interest.
The Leader of the Opposition asked some questions regarding expenditures made in connection with the CF-105. The correct figure is that some $220 million was expended in the research and development of this aircraft prior to this year. In these estimates we have allocated $175 million for the further development of this aircraft which, if it is proceeded with-and we have the right to discontinue it at any time-will carry on development until March 31 of next year.
Reference was made to the proposal for further integration between the logistic and administrative services of the armed forces. The committee recommended that there should be further unification between such services as the chaplain service, medical service and provost service. We are moving in that direction. We have within recent months authorized that all the definitive hospitals should become tri-service hospitals. We have meetings scheduled for the immediate future to see whether it will not be possible to make further progress in the integration of the medical services. Some aspects of the provost services have already been integrated. So far as the chaplain service is concerned, we are seeking authority to appoint a chaplain-general, both Protestant and Roman Catholic, who would supervise that service for all three services.
I must point out to the committee, however, that while there will be some economies effected and I think simpler administration, this integration cannot provide any very significant reduction in the over-all budget. But we are seeking every possible way of saving even small amounts of money.
I cannot agree with the hon. member who spoke on behalf of the C.C.F. group that our defences are completely out of date; that is not so. We have an adequate defence to meet the possible attack of today. We are trying to keep our defences up to date and improve all the time, so we will be able to cope with the means of attack in future years. It would be disturbing and quite incorrect to allow a statement like that to go across the country. It would shatter confidence throughout the land, and I am quite certain that is not correct.
Supply-National Defence
In so far as the cost-sharing of production is concerned, that is more in the realm of defence production than it is a question for the defence department. But I am inclined to agree that we should give very careful consideration, if ever again we go into the production of some complete weapons system, to this aspect of the matter. I do not believe the hon. member speaking for the C.C.F. party was very consistent, because at one point he referred to Canada possibly becoming a subcontractor for the United States in future developments, yet at the same time he agreed we could not go into the production of one complete system. I would hope that it might be possible at some future date, provided we can carry out the research which is necessary and get in on the ground floor, that we might as partners, not as subcontractors, work together in some future production program.
