78. Departmental administration and payments to Canadian Commercial Corporation and other corporate agencies for services provided in connection with defence purchasing and production, $7,232,086.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement in connection with his estimates?

I rise today for the first time, Mr. Chairman, to present the estimates of the Department of Defence Production. I had not thought of making any lengthy statement. I made a detailed statement in committee which I distributed to the members of the committee. In rising I wish to extend, as the Minister of National Defence has done, my thanks to the members of the committee on estimates for the splendid work they have done. I should like also to extend my thanks and appreciation to the chairman of that committee for the preparation made and the manner in which discussions were conducted.
I should like, right at the beginning, to deal with the recommendations which were made by this committee on estimates. In dealing with these suggestions I should like to offer certain explanations which I think the members of this committee should have.
(Translation):
Hon. members of the committee, as this is the first time I am submitting the estimates of my department, I want first of all to ask the hon. members' indulgence. Also, I would like to comment, right at the beginning of my remarks, on the suggestion and advice given by the committee on estimates, where I appeared some time ago.
This is the first time I am presenting my estimates, and I hope to have the opportunity to submit many more in the years to come. This is just a wish I am expressing.
For three years.

I shall now explain in English the decisions taken by the committee on estimates and give the reasons for certain statements. You may be assured that my officials and I are most interested in studying any comments that were made and in making such changes and improvements as members of the committee saw fit to suggest.
(Text):
In dealing with the destroyer escort program the report of the standing committee on estimates raises three questions, as follows; first, the importance of establishing the final unit costs of an individual ship soon after its completion; second, the desirability of introducing in shipbuilding a target plus incentive type of contract; and third, the
[The Deputy Chairman.]
importance of giving the shipbuilding industry increasing opportunities to suggest ways of cost reductions.
These three points discussed in committee are well taken. I would, however, like to comment upon them and to offer the assurance to this house that the Department of Defence Production has taken action on each of them.
In determining the final cost of a ship in the destroyer escort program it must be recognized that we are dealing with a program of 14 identical ships under various stages of construction in seven different shipyards. The determination of final unit costs is influenced by the program characteristics of this construction rather than by the completion of any single ship.
Of the material going into the ships, about 95 per cent is procured centrally and not by the individual shipbuilder. This includes the main engines, boilers, gearing, armament, electronic gear, turbines and related equipment. The total production of these major components extends over the life of the program. Accordingly the determination of final unit costs for such components can be precisely established only after the entire requirement of 14 ship sets is complete. As a result it is possible that the material costs of an individual ship are not likely to be known until the production and cost of components for the entire program is complete.
It would be possible to determine the costs independently of each ship set of components as it is delivered. This, however, would distort the individual shipbuilder's costs. In other words, the first unit of production would bear all the pre-production expenses incurred to that time. For this reason the unit costs of material are averaged over the ships in the program, and can be defined with precision only after all such material costs are known. At the present time eight ships of the destroyer escort program have been accepted. It will not be before the end of 1959 that all the remaining ships in the 14-ship program will be finally accepted.
This delay in the determination of final costs will be reduced in future programs where the development expenses are not significant and material is procured on the basis of a firm price or a variation of the firm price. Although there are other factors which contribute to this delay, I shall not attempt to deal with them at this time. The basic contributing factor is that already discussed.
This department recognizes the difficulties inherent in the cost plus contract. As a result of such experience there was introduced in our last major shipbuilding program

for coastal minesweepers a target plus incentive type of contract. By this and related measures substantial savings were realized in ship construction. By way of illustration, the man hour expenditures on this minesweeper program of six ships were reduced on an average by 30 per cent of those for a previous program for corresponding minesweepers.
In the new destroyer escort program the planning and contractual techniques developed in the minesweeper program referred to will be applied. I am confident that the results will demonstrate substantial economies over our earlier experience.
On the question of improving the liaison with the Canadian shipbuilding industry to the end of achieving reductions in cost, I am in accord with the recommendation of the estimates committee in this connection. In recent years there has been maintained the closest and most intimate liaison with the shipbuilding industry. My department has at all times studied, with units of the shipbuilding industry, problems of scheduling, planning, procurement and production. This has been done not only with individual shipbuilders but also with the Canadian shipbuilding and ship repairing association, by means of committees, consultation, exchange of technical data and other measures. This has at all times had as its objective improved efficiency and lower costs. I would go so far as to say that in few if any branches of industry has there been a more effective exchange of ideas and liaison than the exchange which exists between the Department of Defence Production and the Canadian shipbuilding industry.
Considerable thought has been given to the question of accepting performance bonds and/or pay and performance bonds to secure Defence Construction (1951) Limited contracts. A decision to change to a system of accepting performance bonds has not been reached but is now under review. The considerations affecting the use of such bonds are, first, both the Department of Public Works and Defence Construction (1951) Limited are subject to the government contracts regulations under the Financial Administration Act, which call for security deposits in the form of a certified cheque or government bonds; second, the possibility that general introduction of surety bonds would increase the cost of construction to the crown; third, it is not clear that the use of performance bonds would have as desirable an effect on the satisfactory completion of the work-for example, the incentive to complete the work by a release of cash would be absent-fourth, fear of unwieldiness of
Supply-Defence Production this practice because of the introduction of a third party to contend with in the event of disputes and difficulties in the administration of the contract; fifth, inequality of tendering opportunity, the likely difficulty on the part of small contractors in remote areas in obtaining insurance coverage.
I shall make other comments on the crown assets corporation and other recommendations which have been made by the committee as time progresses.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would like to ask the
minister one or two questions, if I may, but before I do so I am sure the house would want me to extend to him congratulations upon this, his first presentation of the estimates of the Department of Defence Production, and to extend to him best wishes in the performance of his duties in that department. He will be, or so I take it, presenting the estimates of the department for the remainder of this parliament, though I think he will allow me to dissent with his view that that situation should continue after this parliament.
The questions uppermost in my mind are these; first, what ships are entrusted to the minister's department for construction? While I heard him make a statement a moment ago, it was difficult to follow the nature of that statement as he made it and I am interested in knowing which ships now under construction by the government are entrusted for construction to the Department of Defence Production. A statement was made by the Minister of Transport at Kingston some time ago-in fact, to be more exact, during the election campaign-as to a number of ships allocated to various yards prompts me to put this question. Was this done through the Department of Defence Production or through the Department of Transport?
My second question is with respect to the allocation of these ships. How does the department proceed? Is it by way of tender? Does the contract go to the yard submitting the lowest tender, or how?
My third and last question is, are contracts of a fixed nature allocated by the minister's department? I have in mind contracts for a fixed price; are there some cases of a nature not contemplated in the ordinary course of construction in other departments which warrant the granting of a ship contract at a fixed price and, if so, would the minister be good enough to tell the house of any example or examples of which he may know of such case or cases?

In reply to the hon. member for Laurier, I wish to first thank him for his good wishes, though he did not extend them in respect of future parliaments and

Supply-Defence Production in that, of course, I cannot concur. In reply to the first question, the Department of Defence Production generally builds only naval ships for the Department of National Defence. We do not do any building for the Department of Transport. We build the ships that come under national defence. The second question dealt with the allocation of ship contracts to the different shipyards. This is done on the recommendation of the maritime commission. With regard to the third question, contracts for the building of small naval vessels have been awarded on the basis of a fixed price, but the target plus procedure is followed with regard to larger vessels.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do I understand that this commission recommends not only the yard but also the allocation of a fixed or contract price as well? Or is that done in the minister's department.

No. The maritime commission recommends a shipyard. They make a report that a certain yard should have a certain contract at a certain time perhaps because it is out of work and has no contracts on hand. Other yards might be more suitable, but possibly they would have a number of contracts on hand.

I have a word to say about the recommendations of the estimate committee to which the minister has already referred. I take it from the minister's remarks that he has some doubt about the validity or value of recommendation 1(a) on the destroyer escort program, and that in so far as recommendation 1(b) is concerned he believes that the shipbuilding industry has in the past been given full opportunity to consult with the department in respect of ways and means of keeping the cost of ships to a minimum and, that therefore the recommendation in that particular paragraph has already been carried out. I also gather that with regard to the recommendation as to the desirability, which we all share, of making sure that the work for which the department is responsible should go wherever possible to Canadian industry, that the minister is not opposed to this recommendation, of course, but feels that along with the others it is already part of the policy of the department, and that it is in that sense only that he finds they are unacceptable.
In reply to the Leader of the Opposition I would say I agree absolutely with his remarks. It is the policy which has been followed, and we are still following that practice.

I just have a brief question to put to the minister, and one comment to make. On June 30 of this year the

minister made a reply in answer to a question which I put to him previously in writing, question No. 101. The return is to be found at page 1791 of Hansard for June 30. My question was:
1.	Has the government, through the Department of Defence Production, recently awarded contracts for the purchase of trucks from the Ford Motor Company of Canada and from Mercedes-Benz Limited?
2.	If so, how many from each company, and what was the amount of the respective contracts?
The minister was kind enough to reply, and without going into the details of that reply I may say it showed that $592,976.14 was spent in purchases of trucks from a Canadian company, the Ford Motor Company of Canada, and an amount of $363,817.63 for trucks purchased from a foreign corporation manufacturing this product outside of the country and in the country of origin, the company being Mercedes-Benz of Canada Limited.
The minister will understand my concern about this return in the absence of satisfactory explanations. I have in the constituency which I represent, and in the community from which I come, two of the large automobile plants of Canada. It is a community in which, as the minister knows, there continues to be a high level of unemployment at the moment, and it is somewhat difficult in the absence of a satisfactory explanation to understand why there should be these purchases from abroad, particularly when the articles purchased are not intended to be used by Canadian citizens as such but by officials in the employ of the crown in the right of Canada.
I understand that the argument made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to whom a comment was directed some time ago on this subject when his estimates were under consideration, was to the effect that it was necessary to have some balance between what a country bought and what it sold, but it seems to me that at a time like this with so much unemployment it could confidently be argued that we ought to be careful about making purchases of this kind.
The minister will note that in the report of the committee a reference is made in a general way not to this particular matter but to the character of the problem involved. In recommendation 3(2) it is urged by the committee that the Department of Defence Production should distribute purchases as broadly as possible in Canada. Under the rules of the house it was not possible to frame a question in such a way-so I was informed at the time-as to elicit information of a general character which would show whether or not there had been other purchases of this character at that time or since.

I understand that the Department of Defence Production acts simply as a purchasing agent, and it is not a question now of allocating responsibility or blame. But as the minister made this reply I hope he will be in a position to explain to the committee why, at a time when there is so much unemployment, particularly in my area, it should have been found desirable and necessary to purchase trucks and other motor vehicles in the proportions indicated in the reply made to me.
It may be argued that since there are Canadian troops overseas there was more to be gained by purchasing products from a company operating in the area where Canadian troops are located, in the interests of economy, in the interests of saving time and for the sake of efficiency generally. But on examination of the items I find that some of the vehicles purchased from both the Ford Motor Company of Canada and the foreign corporation are of the same type. For instance, on January 24 some 120 3-ton dump trucks were purchased from the Ford Motor Company in the amount of $384,197. Then on April 22 five of the same kind of vehicles were purchased from a foreign corporation, and likewise on May 21 more trucks were purchased. I should be very grateful to the minister if he would give us an explanation of this situation, possibly informing the committee what the practice is going to be in the future.

In reply to the hon. member for Essex East may I state that I know the recommendation made by the committee in this connection was that the department was to purchase as much as possible in Canada. After consulting my officials I am pleased to report to the members of this committee, first, that the vehicles bought during the past year in Europe were bought essentially for our troops overseas. One of the reasons for this given by the officials of my department concerns economy with respect to repairs to the vehicles and the obtaining of parts. If the vehicles are purchased there they can be readily serviced and parts are easily obtainable.
I am greatly in sympathy with the remarks made by the hon. member for Essex East. Together with my officials I shall study this question when I have an opportunity to examine matters of this kind. Our policy is to encourage all industry in Canada. I think perhaps there might be some change in this policy of procuring vehicles for our troops.
The statement I wish to make to the committee in answer to the question with respect to our purchasing in Canada is that it is clearly desirable on economic and strategic grounds that defence production purchases 57071-3-205
Supply-Defence Production be distributed as widely as possible throughout the country. I assure hon. members of the committee that we have considered and shall continue to consider this factor in awarding our contracts within the general context of distributing our purchases for defence production as widely as possible in obtaining supplies and services. I assure the hon. member that my officials and I will certainly study the question.

Mr. Chairman, there is only one point I should like to make, and that is with reference to the comments of the minister concerning performance bonds in defence construction contracts. This matter has given me some concern because of the rather frustrating and bitter experiences I had representing as a solicitor the suppliers of materials and subcontractors for defence projects, where perhaps a general contractor had gone bankrupt or had become involved in certain financial difficulties because of the fact that it is impossible under law to file and maintain a mechanics lien against this type of crown property. It leaves the contractor, the subcontractor and the supplier in a rather difficult position, and one which is much inferior to the position they enjoy when carrying out normal commercial construction.
It may be said this is a calculated risk the contractor or supplier takes; but I would put it to you, Mr. Chairman, that if a contractor or supplier is going to take a calculated risk on this sort of thing he is going to protect himself in some measure by a price increase. I am wondering if the effect of the practice is not to increase the cost to the crown of some of these defence projects by reason of the fact that there is no way through a pay and performance bond or even a straight performance bond of achieving protection.
I would prefer to see established a pay and performance bond. I have seen the effect of such bonds in construction in my own province, and the recommendation of the committee certainly has much to commend it. I have seen the experience of ordinary performance bonds in construction carried on by other departments of the federal government, notably the Department of Public Works. Recently in Edmonton there was a very unfortunate bankruptcy during the construction of a federal building, and if it had not been for a performance bond the Department of Public Works would have been in a most difficult situation and the building program would have been held up for some considerable time.
Fully appreciating the thoughts expressed by the minister as to the value of a cash deposit rather than a performance bond, I would point out that while either answer is

Supply-Defence Production neither totally correct nor totally wrong it does not represent a complete answer. In the case of a cash deposit the contractor must put up 10 per cent of the value of the tender. As we all know, some of the defence contracts are rather extensive and the large sum of money represented by the cash deposit is tied up for some considerable length of time. The contractor has to borrow that money and pay interest on it. The interest is charged to the crown through the tender price.
I am wondering whether the crown is getting as good a deal as it would if it adopted the policy of using pay and performance bonds or ordinary performance bonds. Admittedly the contractor will charge up the premium, but due to the fact that moneys are held on deposit for long periods of time interest must be paid during this time, and I feel an examination would suggest that there might be a greater element of cost to the crown as a result of the practice of requiring a cash deposit by the contractor. I recommend to the minister that most serious consideration be given to the alternatives rather than adhering to the policy of requiring a cash bond. I believe the committee has made a worth-while suggestion in this respect, and I would commend it to the minister.

In reply to the hon. member for Edmonton West, as I said previously public works and Defence Construction Limited are subject to the Financial Administration Act. The comments made by the committee are very worth while. I am informed by my officials that it is not really the responsibility of defence production but it should be a recommendation to the treasury board. I am informed that they are studying the question of performance bonds at the present time.

Item agreed to.
Canadian Arsenals Limited-
83. Administration and operation, $1,800,000.

I wonder if the minister would mind explaining what appears from the form of the estimates to be a new item, No. 83. I understand it is largely a matter of form, but I should appreciate having the minister explain it to the committee.

I shall be glad to do so, Mr. Chairman. In previous years, because much work was being done in the factories of Canadian Arsenals Limited, we did not require this item, vote No. 83. Since the beginning of this year production has constantly been going down, and we do not conceive of there being much amelioration in the months to come. That is the reason this vote is necessary.
Vote 83 is the one I singled out as showing a marked change from last year. These are

the comments I made in committee. I should explain that since its establishment in 1945 one of the responsibilities of Canadian Arsenals Limited has been the maintenance in serviceable condition of certain facilities which were developed under crown ownership during or prior to world war II and which the government wished to conserve.
In the company's early years costs related to this custodial responsibility were defrayed by parliamentary votes. Later, with the development of the defence program because of the Korean crisis, the volume of production work became adequate to meet expenses out of sales and thus a nominal figure of $1 a year was submitted to cover operating costs.
Based on studies during the past several years the company estimates that a minimum economic volume of about $40 million in sales is required each year to permit the company's functions to be carried out on a self-supporting basis. According to the orders currently on hand, a probable sales volume of only $30 million is expected in 1958-59, or 25 per cent less than the above mentioned economic volume. On this basis, the company anticipates a manufacturing loss of some $2,300,000, which is expected to be reduced by miscellaneous revenue of around $500,000, derived mainly from services and rentals, thus producing the net possible requirement for the current year of $1,800,000 as shown in the estimates.
Would the minister mind telling us what plants of Canadian Arsenals are inactive at the moment?

I am informed that none of our plants is out of operation. All of our plants are operating. We keep them all operating as much as possible but on a much lower schedule than before, but all of our plants are going to be kept in operation.

Item agreed to.
541. To provide capital assistance tor the construction, acquisition, extension or improvement of capital equipment or works by private contractors engaged in defence contracts, or by Crown Plants operated on a management-fee basis, or by Crown Companies under direction of the Minister of Defence Production, subject to approval of treasury board-further amount required, $1,200,000.

Mr. Chairman, I have no questions to ask under this item, but since it is the last item of this department I think it should perhaps be put on the record that in the last hour or so we have passed estimates amounting to almost $1,750 million. The reason that we have been able to pass these estimates with such speed should be made clear on the record of Hansard. These estimates have been previously examined by a committee which has worked many hours going into them in detail; otherwise, I am

sure, Mr. Chairman, we would not have been able to get them so quickly. Perhaps that should be on Hansard.
Item agreed to.

DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE 383. Departmental administration, $282,666.

Mr. Chairman, last night at ten o'clock I had started to make some remarks with respect to the relationship between the employees of the federal government and their employer, namely the federal government, and was suggesting that those employees who, as I said, I would like to call public employees rather than the degrading name of civil servants, should be placed in substantially the same position as are employees of private industry, or as employees of any of the crown corporations particularly. They should have the right to organize into a union of their choice, which apparently they have and, following that, be allowed the same privileges, rights and responsibilities as are employees of crown corporations, in that the organization that they may join can apply for certification of bargaining authority under the federal labour act and be in a position to enter into negotiations with their employer, the federal government, in somewhat the same manner as do employees of crown corporations, such as the C.N.R. You might expect that the ultimate result of negotiations conducted in this fashion, if no satisfactory settlement is reached across the bargaining table, or with the assistance of a conciliation board, would be either a strike by or a lockout of our public employees. I am sure that many of them do not want to extend this type of relationship to the point of there being the possibility of a strike or a lockout.
There is a general understanding prevalent in the country at the moment, I think, that public employees and employees of the federal government do not have the right to walk out on strike. I would submit that that same impression was prevalent with respect to the British Columbia government employees up until last year when the organization of the British Columbia government employees, because of the difficulties they got into and because of their inability to get any satisfactory answer or solutions from the government of that province, decided that they would go out on strike. They did not reach the stage of ending up in a strike but nevertheless we now realize that in so far as the province of British

Supply-Secretary of State Columbia is concerned, the employees of the provincial government of that province do have the right to strike. I assume the same situation exists with respect to the federal government but I am not suggesting that the establishment of some sensible negotiating procedure for our public employees in the federal field should extend to that end, and I am sure that they would not want it to extend to that end, either.
We can look at the position of firefighters employed by municipalities. In effect those employees as firefighters are in no position different from that of the employees of the federal government except that their employer is a different person. Firefighters work for a municipality and are therefore in the public service. Federal government employees work for the federal government of Canada and they are in the public service. I might add that other municipal employees are likewise in the same position. They have had established for them a procedure somewhat similar to that which I am suggesting at the moment. There should be a change in our attitude toward public employees and we should give them the same rights, responsibilities and privileges or substantially the same rights, responsibilities and privileges, I should say, in labour-management relations as have employees working for crown corporations, municipalities or private employers.
I know that this approach has been advanced in years past just as it is being advanced now. I submit that there is just as much validity to the argument in favour of this type of arrangement as there has been in any of the years in the past, and I hope the minister will undertake to express an opinion in this regard and announce some policy that will allow employees in the public service of Canada the right to conduct their discussions relating to wages, working hours, dismissals and grievances and so on, in a fashion that will permit an amicable solution to be found.
I submit that generally speaking there is no channel for finding solutions for some of these problems. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that in recent days there was a discussion respecting the discharge of an employee in the Department of Agriculture working in the Montreal area. That is merely one case which has been discussed and it points up the necessity of providing some channel through which sensible discussion of these matters can take place. If there is failure after such discussion takes place then these matters should be placed in the hands of an outside tribunal to make a decision not only with

Supply-Secretary of State respect to grievances arising from discharge but with respect to other conditions of employment.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to thank hon. members who were kind enough to express to me their good wishes on the occasion of my birthday. I was indeed touched by their kind words in wishing a prompt recovery for my wife. I can assure my hon. friends that their gracious consideration and kind words are much appreciated.
I will make a statement to the hon. member for Skeena when we are discussing the civil service commission but I should like to answer the remarks that the hon. member for Ottawa East made yesterday. In the course of general remarks which the hon. member for Ottawa East made in the house on the seventh instant with respect to the estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State, the civil service commission, the office of the chief electoral officer and the department of public printing and stationery, the hon. member inquired as to the progress of the work of the royal commission on patents, copyrights, trade-marks and industrial designs.
Hon. members will recall that on June 10, 1958, pursuant to an inquiry directed to me by the hon. member for Ottawa East, I tabled the commission's report on copyrights. I am now pleased to announce that the commission's report on industrial designs was submitted to and accepted by the governor in council on the seventh instant and will be deposited with the Clerk of the house today. As to the commission's next report, which will deal with patents of invention, it is not expected to be submitted before some time next year, in the spring, it is hoped.
It has already been explained many times in the house that the assignment of the royal commission was of considerable magnitude and complexity and that the members of the commission can devote only a part of their time to this assignment as they have to continue the discharge of their normal functions. I should perhaps add that inquiries of this sort in other countries, in the United Kingdom, for instance, have usually extended over a considerable period of time.

I am very happy that the report on industrial designs will be tabled today. Is the personnel of the commission the same or have any of the members resigned? I noticed that the minister did not indicate anything about trade-marks.

We do not know yet if we will have anything on trade-marks but I would say to the hon. member that the members of the commission on industrial designs are the same. One man has resigned but has acted until the completion of the report.

I appreciate the comment of the minister that probably questions relating to public employees should be dealt with under the vote for the civil service commission. I had intended to deal with the matter under that vote except that it was raised last night and I thought it might be well to have a continuity of comment. I should like to suggest that the minister should consider one other matter with regard to the relationships between the federal government and its employees and perhaps he might comment on it on the civil service commission vote. I understand that so far as some of the employees of some of the crown corporations are concerned a system has been developed of establishing wage rates and relationships between wage rates which is commonly referred to as a job evaluation program or a co-operative wage study as it is known in other circles.
While I do not intend to give blanket en-dorsation to every type of job evaluation program that has been developed, most of them in private industry, nevertheless I feel that if a job evaluation program is developed by negotiation between employees and employer and is established on sound, scientific principles for determining wage rates and differences between categories it may be most beneficial both for the employees and the employer, in this case the federal government. I suggest that we should consider the establishment of a job evaluation program for federal government employees. I do not mean that it should be developed by the government and then imposed on the employees as a fait accompli. The government should not say, "Here is the plan that we have developed." I do not think that is a sensible way to develop such a program.

But if the federal government is desirous of entering into such a job evaluation program, and I commend the general idea very highly although not all types of such programs, then it should be done only by negotiation and discussion with the organizations representing the employees in the manner and spirit of collective bargaining so that the manual or base on which the program works will be agreed upon mutually first before it is put into effect. I would say also that such a program requires a fairly large degree of acceptance, probably 75 to 80 per cent of the employees affected, if the plan is to be of any great benefit. I reiterate that if the government is going to go into the field, and I suggest that it should, a plan should not be imposed upon the employees but that it should be negotiated with their representatives and, second, that there should be a pretty high percentage of acceptance by the employees themselves. This is one other facet of the question, in addition to that of the procedure of negotiation, with which I dealt earlier, upon which I hope the minister will comment when the civil service vote is under consideration.

I have some specific questions I want to ask concerning the chief electoral officer and the civil service, but there was one general suggestion that I wished to make. I could make it to the Minister of Justice, the Minister of National Revenue, or the Secretary of State. I make it to the Secretary of State because he is the one who filed the answer to a question I asked about those books which, in the past year, had been banned from Canada because the people in the Department of National Revenue felt they were not up to the proper standard.
This whole question of the censorship of books, especially obscene literature, is one that is very much to the fore. It has been mentioned by quite a number of members. The suggestion I wanted to make to the Secretary of State was this. The list I received only covered the books that were banned within the last year. There is a much more extensive list, possibly covering 500 books. In the short list I received there were several books that I had read, some of which were out and out smut and had no business being in the country. Their literary merit was nil. This is my opinion, of course, and I expect it could be challenged by other people.
Since it is likely there will be legislation introduced next year concerning this question, I thought it might be a good idea for the Secretary of State to make arrangements to obtain copies of all of those books that
Supply-Secretary of State have been banned by our so-called censorship authorities, not for general reading at all, but so that members of parliament could look at what has been decided in the past as being improper or unfit for Canadians to read. We would, in this way, get a much better idea of how the system has worked in the past. There have been many complaints about the system; that it has been a hit or miss affair; that it has been applied by men without any literary judgment, and so on. It seems to me that by adopting this suggestion we would bring home to members of parliament just what has been considered dangerous or bad reading for Canadians. It would give us a chance to assess, quite frankly, some of the various degrees of pornography, some of which are interwoven with aspects of literature.
I believe the Secretary of State would be the minister to do this because he tends to interrelate the activities of a number of departments in an official way. I would not make any official recommendation as to what should be done with the books after legislation has been introduced and after members of parliament have read them. I am not making this suggestion that the books be acquired in order to get members of parliament to read them, although I am sure they will show considerable interest in the rather delightful batch or miscellany that will be produced.
The points I want to make in connection with the civil service are highly derivatory. There are some suggestions made by Dr. J. J. Deutsch in an article entitled "Some Thoughts on the Public Service", which appeared in February, 1957. There are several good suggestions in this article. This gentleman worked for the public service for over 20 years, and is at present engaged by the University of British Columbia. The point that appealed to me most was his feeling that one of the prime difficulties with the civil service was that really exceptional talent did not rise to the top quickly. In his article he says:
Alongside this problem of machinery there is the matter of selecting and bringing along outstanding talent. It is my impression that this is not being done early enough or fast enough. There is too much of what the Germans call Gleichschaltung- too much holding back to the pace of the average. It is the common complaint of those who consider the civil service for a career that advancement is too slow. There may not be much substance in this complaint in the general case, but in the case of exceptional ability it is very important.
I have noticed that the gentlemen who come into the civil service with a background of Rhodes' scholarship rise with remarkable speed to the top of the public service. I have no derogatory comments to make about

Supply-Secretary of State Rhodes scholars in any way or about their background. One of the points that I would make is that the reason they do advance so quickly lies not only in the talent that they have but through their prestige and status, given by these scholarships. There is a label on them when they go into the public service to the effect that these boys are good, so they get somewhere. I have the feeling that many people who go into the public service may have ability and talent, but because they have not that little prestige label they do not advance so quickly. I believe this particular point is worth some consideration by the civil service commission.
Mr. Deutsch goes on to give this expression of opinion:
On the other hand, I do not believe there is anywhere a more impersonal organization than the civil service. The individual cannot locate anywhere the heart and conscience of the organism. There is no proprietor or general manager in the usual sense. The employee has to fall back upon rules and regulations, and, in his collective capacity, upon the passage of resolutions directed to the governing authorities and the general public. For the general body of the service there are no employee unions in the sense in which they exist in private industry. Consequently it is necessary to develop special machinery. The establishment of the national joint council has been a very important step. It is vital that the work of this council should be successful.
Then the author goes on to suggest that within departments personnel officers be given a much higher status in order that they could begin to breathe a bit of heart and personality into the machine to give the people within the service, to whom it is exceptionally impersonal and mechanical, a feeling that human considerations are very much to the fore. I would imagine that if hon. members and the minister have not had an opportunity of glancing at this piece of writing it would be worth while if the Secretary of State were to look at these general suggestions, bearing in mind what the hon. member for Skeena did bring to his attention as well as to the attention of the civil service commission.

The hon. member's suggestion that certain books banned by the Department of National Revenue be acquired by the library of parliament is one for consideration of the joint committee on the parliamentary library.
So far as the civil service commission is concerned, I would deal with this matter when the estimates of the department are called.

I am a member of the joint committee on the library of parliament and I was going to make the suggestion there, but I felt that if these books were acquired we would be leaving ourselves open to the appearance of suggesting that they become a

permanent part of the book stock of the library of parliament. Obviously, most of them should not be given house room in any library. However, I think the members of parliament should have an opportunity to judge these books, and that is why I made the suggestion to the minister.
I should like to congratulate the minister on the way in which he has managed to slip out of becoming the custodian of pornographic literature as well as the custodian of enemy property.

Mr. Chairman, I have just one remark to make in respect to the statement of the hon. member for Port Arthur in which he advanced the proposition that people in the public service should advance in accordance with their ability. The hon. member for Port Arthur some days ago had occasion to remark that the proposition I put to the house contained some pretty good socialism, and I would like to say to him, through you, Mr. Chairman, that the subject about which the hon. member has been speaking seems to me like pretty good free enterprise.
The indication of the remark of the hon. member who has just spoken is that he thinks that is the situation. That is self-explanatory.
It's a good thing he thinks -a lot of you fellows don't even think.

That is a fair amount of income. I suppose it would be possible to determine just how much surplus is embodied in that figure, although I think it would be difficult to assess the costs of this division. In the

Perhaps one year might be too short a time, but I think very shortly after the lapse of 12 months many of these records could be put on microfilm, which would increase the available space.
I am informed by my officers that the files are kept for five years because they are required for that length of time.

386.	Bureau for translations, $1,462,120.

Mr. Chairman, I notice that the strength of the bureau of translations has been increased by one, from 294 to 295, and that the number of translators within that bureau has been increased by the same number. I think we all are very conscious of the importance of this bureau and of the necessity to secure translations of official

Supply-Secretary of State documents with the minimum of delay. Sometimes when delay occurs, as it is bound to occur, the fault is not in the bureau but in the fact that there are not enough translators there to do the work which is required and to do it as quickly as we would like. I want to ask the minister if he thinks that the strength of the bureau, which has now been increased by one, is sufficient to deal with the work required and to deal with it at reasonable speed.
It has been increased in the supplementary estimates by 11 employees.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I follow that up with another observation. It has been noticed in this house from time to time that there are some publications which are not translated into the French language and the question which occurs to me at the moment is why this should be the case. Further, as the Leader of the Opposition has said, there are instances where though the reports and publications are translated they are not translated concurrently with the English version, and I presume, although I do not know, that this is so because of the lack of translators. The Secretary of State has just said that in the supplementary estimates another 11 translators will be added. Does he think this number will be sufficient in view of the questions I have asked and in view, also, of another measure which is on the order paper, namely, the measure having to do with simultaneous translation? Is that a matter which will be the responsibility of the Secretary of State? Will he be charged with the responsibility for the specialized translators who will be required for this work, because I am sure that the Secretary of State has been at the United Nations and has seen the very highly specialized work that this entails. It is work of a difficult character, as he knows, and the question which arises in my mind at the moment is whether this will be his responsibility and, if this is the case, whether he is giving some consideration to this matter which all of us in this committee will agree is one of great moment.

I am informed that the translation bureau is a service of the house. The bureau translates only when it is asked to do so. It does not come under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State. Each minister can ask for translations, and translations are made when the bureau is asked to make them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What about the other questions I asked?
I am informed that eight interpreters are training at the present time and they will be ready pretty soon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is that eight out of the eleven?
Eight out of the eleven.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I pursue this question a bit further? What are the qualifications which are going to be required of these translators-I say specialized translators but perhaps I should not use that expression, but I presume a great deal more will be required of them than of the others-over and above those required for the present translators in the department?
Their qualifications are a knowledge of English and French, a knowledge of the procedure of the house and of the terminology used.

I take it from what the minister has now said that the additional strength of the bureau of translation to deal with the work which has been normally done by this bureau in the past is four, because eight out of the eleven provided for in the supplementary estimates will be doing simultaneous translations in the house, I take it also from what the minister has said that he considers this number to be sufficient to deal with the requests which are made to the bureau for translation services, and we know how important that work is and how valuable it is. The eight who are being provided for the simultaneous translation service of the house will be covered, I take it, by the supplementary vote we are coming to. The total amount of that vote would indicate, however, that the average salary to be paid to these simultaneous translators would be somewhere around $5,000. This is very skilled and very difficult work to do accurately, as those of us who have been at the United Nations realize, it is a very important kind of work. I know, as perhaps the minister may know, that in New York they have not found it easy to get qualified simultaneous translators although the amount that is provided as salary down there is about double that provided for in the supplementary estimates. I mention this matter to the Secretary of State because it will be important that these men should be highly qualified. I hope this is being taken into consideration in training people for this work.

I am informed that the department has recommended having six more translators for the translation bureau. The amount provided in the supplementary estimates is only for nine months, and the rate of salary will be around $7,000.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask another question dealing with the matter I brought up earlier in connection with those publications or documents of the house which are not translated into the French language? The minister gave the formal reply which is that his department translate what they are asked to translate, and 1 have no fault to find with that. But does the minister not think that he should go a bit further, since he has the translators at his disposal in his department, and say that when it is brought to his attention, as is being done now, and as has been done from time to time in the house, that there are publications which are not being translated into French or publications that are not being translated simultaneously with the English version when it appears such, does he not think that he should bring this to the attention of his colleagues in an endeavour to see that the English and French documents are tabled simultaneously?
I will be very glad to deal with this matter.

Patent and copyright office-
387.	Administration division, $144,650.
Mr. Chairman, once again I speak about these reports. The minister said a while ago that the report had been tabled in May-
Yes.

For 1957-58. I wish I had a copy. In any event my first comment on patent administration is that I am aware of the fact that there is a royal commission investigating the Patent Act and I quite appreciate that it will take some time before we have a final report from the royal commission in this regard. I appreciate also that it will take some time before we have the final report of the royal commission in that regard.
One thing that very quickly strikes the eye of one who looks at these reports is the fact that generally speaking the number of applicants for patents who are Canadian citizens is very small compared with the total number of applications filed in any one year. In the period 1957-58 there were 22,257 applications for patents filed of which I believe 1,154 were Canadian. If my figures are correct they indicate that something in the nature of 5 per cent are applications from Canadians. One might say immediately that we in Canada are maintaining a patent system for people who reside outside of Canada, if one wanted to make that kind of statement. I have no real objection to the fact that
Supply-Secretary of State applications for patents are granted to citizens of other countries. That is the system that has always existed and unless for some good reason of which I am not aware at present the commissioners decide to recommend otherwise I suppose it will continue.
My point is this. I am interested in knowing what is the effect on Canadian trade of granting patents to so many people outside of Canada. That is why I put those questions to the Minister of Justice and once to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I will also ask the Secretary of State to ascertain whether within the royal commission itself there have been or will be any inquiries to find out in what manner the Patent Act affects trade in Canada. It is very evident that all important patents except perhaps those granted to the research council and the atomic energy commission and a few others in this country are granted to foreign citizens. The holding of patents can restrict trade and control prices. My main request of the minister is that he direct the attention of [DOT] the royal commission to this fact and insist upon a better study of the working sections of the Patent Act, that is those sections which require that a patent shall be worked in Canada. I am afraid that too few people realize the monopoly which is created in foreign hands by the use of our patent system. With these few remarks concerning that feature of the Patent Act I shall leave the subject.
I would point out to the committee, however, that over the past few years the department has shown a deficit in income which decreased from $95,000-odd in 1953-54 to $279,000-odd in 1956-57. I do not have the comparative figure for 1957-58 immediately at hand but in any event it also shows a larger decrease. The crux of the matter is this. The deficit is due to the expenditure incurred in the printing of patents. The department incurs a large deficit because it prints its patents and that expense will recur from year to year. I should like to have the comments of the minister as to whether in light of these facts he still considers that our system of printing these patents is in the public interest and of sufficient value to warrant the expenditure. There is very little income through the sale of copies of patents. The total income in 1956-57 through the sale of copies was $86,000-odd according to the figures I have and the net loss was about $650,000. It is a matter that bears some investigation. As far as the printing done by the printing bureau is concerned it is of an excellent quality and involves complicated technical work. The actual cost of the printing is comparable with the cost



Supply-Secretary of State of work done in outside firms and I am merely questioning the principle of whether we should continue having a loss charged to that department which, as I said, amounted to $650,000 in 1956-57.
I feel that my remarks should be brief but, of course, I should like some comment from the minister as to whether he feels the technical staff is sufficient for the administration of this act and as to whether he has received any suggestions from the commissioner of patents concerning improvements.
Before taking my seat I must not forget to deal with one of my main bones of contention and that is the fact that the patent office has been moved to No. 8 temporary building near the experimental farm. If any hon. members have had to deal with patents in the past I know they will agree with me that this was a great mistake initiated by the previous government, I hasten to admit, but confirmed by the present government. There is no reason why this office should be bandied about from one place to another. It is the only place of record of Canadian inventions in this country. It is an important office where the public deals with the government from day to day and there was no valid reason for moving it from the centre of the city. The minister is not responsible for this but I suggest he could make a name for himself in the future by insisting that one of the initial projects undertaken by the Department of Public Works be the construction somewhere in the centre of Ottawa of a building to house the patents, trade-marks and copyright office.

Mr. Chairman, in dealing with the matter raised by the hon. member for Ottawa East about the deficit, I should like to say that a deficit is inevitable if the fee which is now $60 per patent is to remain the same. The high cost of printing and salaries are the principal reasons for the deficit in so far as expenditures are concerned.
Our deficit for 1957-58 is about one-third of our revenue whereas the deficit of the United States patent office for the year ending June 30, 1957 is more than 140 per cent. It may be of interest to state that in the United Kingdom where the fee is as high as $370 per patent including annual fees the deficit for 1956 is slightly less than 5 per cent of the income. In any event it is felt that no attempt should be made to eliminate or reduce our deficit through an increase of fees or through a decrease of our expenditures which would involve a radical change in our present system until the commission has submitted its recommendation. There are at present 11 vacant patent examiner positions three of which will be filled shortly, and since the

recruitment period is now over very few additional patent examiners will be recruited during the balance of the current financial year. These vacant positions are often used to meet needs that were unforeseen when the estimates were prepared before the start of the fiscal year. For instance, some of those vacant positions of patent examiners are presently being used for students hired as assistant patent examiners for the summer.
As far as the building is concerned, I am informed that in the near future we will have a new building.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word at this stage about the civil service commission. I need not point out to the Secretary of State that he has jurisdiction over a very important group of employees of the government of Canada and that, apart from those who come directly under him, there are a very large number of federal employees who, while not coming under the minister's jurisdiction, nevertheless benefit from the provisions of the Civil Service Commission Act.
During the present session and even before, some of the Secretary of State's colleagues have been making very unkind remarks with respect to members of the civil service. Indeed they stated that certain civil servants were lazy and did not acquit themselves of their duties. They also made other statements which I do not

intend repeating here for fear of detaining the committee. I did feel at the time however-and I think that a large majority of the members of the House of Commons as well as the Secretary of State himself must have shared that feeling-that those statements were altogether unfair and should never have been made. Under the circumstances, it seems that the question which must be put is this. Aware as he is of the statements made, does the Secretary of State feel they are true? If so, what action has he taken to ascertain the truth, if any, of those remarks? If they are inaccurate, as I have every reason to believe, would the Secretary of State be so kind as to make a statement on the matter?

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) for raising that point. Yesterday evening three other hon. members referred to the civil service commission and since their remarks were made in English, the hon. member for Laurier who is perfectly bilingual, will allow me to give my prepared statement with regard to the civil service commission in the same language.
(Text):
Before commenting on the observations on the civil service which were made last evening by the hon. members for Ottawa East, Hull and Skeena and this afternoon by the hon. member for Laurier, I feel I should say a few words in reference to the relationship of the government in general and the Secretary of State in particular to the civil service commission. Confusion on this subject continues to persist in many quarters.
Under the law, the civil service commission is responsible not to the ministry but to parliament. The Secretary of State in no sense administers either the civil service or the commission. He is simply the spokesman designated by the government to report to parliament on the commission's behalf and to act in the capacity in which I am now acting, namely to present to parliament the commission's annual estimates of expenditure and to recommend their approval on behalf of the government. This independence of the civil service commission is at the heart of the arrangements established by the Civil Service Act of 40 years ago. It is essential to the preservation of the merit principle on which the Canadian service is based and to which this government attaches the highest importance.
Both the hon. member for Ottawa East and the hon. member for Hull, and this afternoon the hon. member for Laurier, spoke of the high quality of the civil service of Canada. The present government is fully appreciative
Supply-Secretary of State of this fact and the Prime Minister and other colleagues of mine have had many occasions, in and out of this house, to pay tribute to the loyalty, devotion and efficiency of the great body of men and women who have made their careers in the direct service of the nation. This, however, is not to say that improvements cannot be made in our law and practice with respect to civil service matters and it is with this in view that the government asked the civil service commissioners to make their current thoroughgoing review of the present act, regulations and procedures. Incidentally, their report is expected to be in the government's hands by the end of the year.
The hon. member for Ottawa East made a number of suggestions in connection with this current review, such as a clearer definition of the commission's powers and duties, its relationship to the financial controls exercised by treasury board, improved procedures for selection and for appeals on promotions. He also spoke of the commission's role in regard to working conditions. I can assure my hon. friend that these questions are now under very active examination by the commissioners and that they will take seriously into account his observations on these and other topics in preparing their recommendations to the government.
With regard to salary and wage levels in the civil service, as hon. members will know the recommendations which under the law the commission is required to make to the government are made not through the Secretary of State but through the Minister of Finance.
The hon. member for Ottawa East made a reference to the value in a Canadian civil servant of a knowledge of our two national tongues. He felt that such knowledge should be taken into proper account in selecting men and women for appointment. As he cannot fail to know, I share warmly his views in this respect, and I am informed that the present commissioners have a lively appreciation of the value of bilingualism in the service.
The hon. member for Hull referred at some length to what he described, I think, as a "malaise" prevalent among certain civil servants. He seemed to imply that there was an impression abroad that under the present government civil servants were subject to unfair attack and had some sense of insecurity. He said a good deal about the duty of the minister to be the champion and defender of civil servants. Such fears, if they exist, are wholly without foundation. As I have already said, the present government respects and supports, and intends to

Supply-Secretary of State continue to respect and support the independent status of the civil service commission and a civil service selected and administered on the basis of quality and merit. There will be no change in these respects in any legislation that will be introduced into parliament by this administration.
In reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena concerning the extension to the public service of a greater voice-incidentally, I cannot share his distaste for the traditional and honourable term "civil servant" -I can do no better than to quote as I now do what the Prime Minister said on this subject in an address he delivered on May 1 of this year to the civil service association of Canada:
I believe that civil servants, through representatives of their organizations, should have a greater voice in the process of determining civil service salaries. There should be a more systematic method of bringing your views and your information to bear in the application of those principles of salary policy on which there is already a wide measure of agreement.
1 think this improvement can be achieved within the general framework of institutions and laws which we have already. What is needed is more opportunity and better arrangements for your representatives to sit down at a table with officials representing the government and with officers of the civil service commission, having the essential facts and figures before them, to discuss in detail the comparisons between civil service salaries in various classifications and the pay for similar work in private employment. From this I would hope a common understanding could emerge; and will provide for a better understanding.
Several of my colleagues are working now on this question, as is the civil service commission, and I hope that it will be possible to proceed with improvements along this line in the near future.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the house will welcome the statement the Secretary of State has made. I am sure it will have the effect of relieving to a large extent many of those who have felt embarrassed by some of the incidents that have been taking place in the house within the last short while. I do not want to go back to those incidents and certainly I do not want to discuss any individual case at this stage, but I should like to go a step further and discuss the matter in a general way.
I think the minister was in the house the other day when there was put on Hansard the practice of the house down through the years with reference to political patronage and the dismissal of employees of the civil service, both the outside service and the inside service. That policy was outlined by former leaders of the House of Commons including the late Sir Robert Borden, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Mackenzie King, Lord Bennett and others. The practice which was established during those years was that a member of the civil service should not be dismissed from public office without a certificate of a member of

parliament, in other words, without a member of parliament stating that of his own personal knowledge he was aware that a member of the service had taken part in political activities.
While I put that on the record at the time I did not in any way condone it. On the contrary, I think my remarks indicated that I did not condone that kind of practice and I am wondering whether the minister has given any consideration to the changing, indeed, the modernization of that practice which has become obsolete and which in fact is so unfair, having regard to the circumstances under which we live today, as to demand immediate change. I believe there is no other way in which I can bring this up in the house than under the estimates of the Secretary of State, whose department is responsible for this group of employees.
I think that the time has come to give consideration to the changing of this policy, this old resolution, this tradition which has grown up over the years and to substitute in lieu thereof something more in keeping with our day and age, certainly to substitute in lieu thereof a public hearing or an inquiry by an impartial tribunal when charges of this kind are made. It seems to me to be entirely unconscionable that we should be dealing in 1958 with dismissals from the public service, be it the civil service of Canada or the outside service, of those who are prevailing rate employees, of those who are casual employees or who benefit from the advantages of superannuation, sick benefits according to this obsolete practice.
It would seem to me that the time has come when this outdated and outmoded practice should be brought to an end. The point I should like to make now is that if the minister has not given the matter consideration I believe he should, and I believe that it should be determined how in the future the services of any civil servant, any member of the public service of Canada who is accused of political activity or against whom any other accusation is made in the performance of his duties, might be dispensed with. I trust that the minister is not one of those who would condone conduct whereby an employee of the public service would lose his employment and thereby his livelihood without proper consideration being given to the circumstances of dismissal, without an impartial tribunal being charged with the responsibility of hearing the evidence pro and con so that a fair decision, having regard to all the circumstances, might be rendered.

I appreciate very much the comments of the Secretary of State, especially his quotation from the address by the Prime Minister which in a general way sounds very

good. But I should like to make some inquiries with respect to specific procedures. I would point out that submissions have been made by the civil service federation of Canada through the civil service commission regarding improvements in the act and the regulations. Incidentally, this material was just given to me and I find on looking through it very quickly that it coincides with the suggestions I made earlier regarding negotiation procedure.
I wonder whether we could not have a clearer indication of the attitude of the government because even though, as he says, the minister acts only in the capacity of reporting to parliament on the estimates of the civil service commission, the Civil Service Act comes under the authority of the cabinet which makes suggestions in so far as changes are concerned. I would appreciate, and I am sure the civil service federation and other federal government employee organizations would appreciate, knowing what the attitude of the government is with respect to their specific suggestion about negotiation procedures; their suggestions with respect to outside tribunals dealing with grievances for which no satisfactory settlement is reached. I think we should have a clearer understanding of the attitude of the government in this regard, rather than a reiteration of the general statement of the Prime Minister.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, following the remarks we made yesterday, the minister seems to have understood that we wanted him to intervene directly with the civil service commission. If we gave him that impression, we regret it. For my part, at least, I meant exactly the contrary. I am convinced that the civil service commission is independent and that it should remain so. What we requested was that the minister, who is responsible for the adoption of the estimates of the commission by this house, act also as the protector of the civil service commission and civil servants who depend on him when they are attacked unfairly.
Some hon. members-I am not talking about the minister personally, who has always been very tactful with civil servants-but some hon. members-especially one whose name I do not remember and whose constituency I would not dare mention, but who comes from the far west-attacked civil servants in an exceedingly violent fashion, so much so that at one point the Prime Minister had to step in. Other hon. members, without making direct remarks, indulged in interjections in some debates, by shouting and saying that it was true or false, according to the way they felt about it. That, I think, is
Supply-Secretary of State what creates a certain uneasiness, especially when a minister takes it upon himself to dismiss a civil servant and to accuse him in this house of being guilty of irregularities, if not of plain dishonesty, then refuses to produce evidence of the civil servant's guilt, all this without ordering an inquiry where the man could have had an opportunity to defend himself. This uneasiness is all the greater for having been created by a member of the cabinet. That is why I urge the Secretary of State to ask his cabinet colleagues to safeguard civil servants' rights to defend themselves when they are attacked.
As I said yesterday, if they are guilty, they should be dismissed. I am not in favour of keeping in the civil service people who do not deserve to hold a position in the public service, but it is necessary that they be granted a serious and impartial inquiry where they would have a chance to defend themselves, in order to find out whether or not they are really guilty.
I would have liked to deal with the matter of promotions. I know however that the commission is carrying out a very thorough study of this matter. In fact it is probable that early next session we might review the whole Civil Service Act. Any lengthy remarks in this regard would therefore be premature. We know that, at the present time, when an employee has applied for promotion, the rating given by the department involved might reverse the decision taken by the commission on the basis of the promotion competition. Needless to say, this can at times give rise to unfairness because of certain particular and personal considerations involved between certain applicants and the responsible official of the department concerned, and the civil service commission cannot interfere.
I will leave it at that. I bring up the matter so that when the legislation comes up for review, we will be able to deal with that aspect of the question.

Mr. Chairman, when I said that certain hon. members seemed unaware of the fact that I am merely spokesman for the civil service commission, I did not have the hon. member for Hull in mind. He is too politically wise to be credited with such intentions. I made the statement, in a general way for the benefit of hon. members, especially the new ones, who had the impression that I was in charge of the civil service commission. I wanted to make it clear to them that I am merely spokesman for the commission.
As I have no wish to overstate the point, I will answer the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) in French. Though the hon.

gentleman did not refer to any specific case, as the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) had done, he did make certain remarks which enabled us to guess what he had in mind. Now I understand that the case familiar to everyone does not come under the civil service commission.
I am told that this particular employee did not come under the jurisdiction of the civil service commission which is governed by a very clear section as regards political activity by any of its employees.
Section 55 states that an employee of the civil service commission has no right to meddle in politics.
The hon. member for Laurier will understand that, after having administered and studied that department for two months, I am not yet familiar enough with the situation to carry on a long discussion, but I am informed that, in the case under discussion, when the minister-this has always been recognized- when the minister is in possession of an affidavit stating that this or that employee of this or that department has meddled in politics, he is empowered to dismiss him. speechtext: We in this group have for a number of years opposed the passing by this House of Commons of these bills as private members' bills. The house in committee on Bill No. SD-157, for the relief of Stella Rachel Cater Harris- Mr. McCleave-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

This particular bill has one rather serious feature and that is that these people were married on October 8, 1955 and the lady is alleged to have left her husband less than one year later. Both parties are relatively young, and it seems regrettable that people who were married in 1955 and who were parted some eleven months later should now already be the subject of a bill before the parliament of Canada in which there is a request for a release from their marriage vows at least as far as the law is concerned.
I should like to point out that it is very often said that we grant divorces to these people in the parliament of Canada. We do no such thing. We do not recognize divorce. In taking these actions all we achieve in effect is to relieve the petitioners from being liable to a bigamy charge should he or she remarry.
We relieve them of their legal obligations. That is altogether different from the granting of a divorce although it may be recognized as such. In light of the fact that these people lived together only 11 months, may I ask the chairman of the committee if there is any possibility of a reconciliation and if he knows what efforts have been made toward obtaining a reconciliation?

Mr. Chairman, if the evidence in this case is properly reported in the report of the committee of the other place, we have here a marriage in which the woman -I was going to say was in her autumn years but it would be impolite to refer to a lady's age in that fashion-was in the late summer of life. In other words, these people were not youngsters when they married. The hon. member is perfectly right when he pointed out they did live together less than a year. In that time apparently they could not strike accord. The evidence was that the husband was drinking and on one occasion she entered the front door and he went out
