the back door with another woman. I suppose they established their incompatibility early. The standard question about reconciliation was asked in this case and what I perhaps could describe as the standard answer was given to the effect that she did not feel it would be possible to reconcile with him.
I do not know what efforts are made in these cases to effect a reconciliation. In this case the evidence does not say that a minister or friend of the family was called in to assist this couple to get together. That might have happened but it does not appear in the record.
Were there any detectives in this case? If so, how many detectives were there? Who were they?
There were detectives in this case; once again the firm of Wiseman and Wiseman.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the remarks made by the sponsor of the bill. I realize something of the difficulty he has when as the sponsor of these bills he has to spend so much of his time reading all the information that comes to him in order to properly discharge his responsibility. The evidence contains the following question:
How long did you know your husband before you married him?
As recorded at page 10 of the evidence the reply was as follows:
I went out with him for about a year before we were married.
The hon. member is perfectly right when he says these people were no longer young. The woman is 40 so she must have been about 36 or 37 when she began going out with this man. She went out with him for a whole year and then she married him and almost immediately they found that married life was extremely difficult. I should like to call the hon. member's atention to page 11 of the evidence where Senator Thorvaldson asked the woman the following question:
You couldn't take what, his late nights, the fact of him coming home late?
The reply was as follows:
Carrying on with other women ... I couldn't live with a man who was going out with other women and carrying on.
This indicates a continuing process of misconduct on the husband's part. It is most unusual that this should be referred to as a continuing error or transgression. She had known him and gone out with him for a year before the marriage and less than a year after the marriage she referred to his behaviour in

this fashion. Again she was asked the following questions and gave the following answers with respect to the possibility of a reconciliation as reported at page 11 of the evidence:
Q. Is there any chance of a reconciliation?
A. No.
Q. Would you forgive him?
A. No.
I wonder if the hon. member would care to comment on whether it is possible in his province and in most provinces of Canada to obtain a divorce when there has been little effort made toward reconciliation?

Before answering the question, Mr. Chairman, may I point out the danger of discussing these cases in this house, in doing so we are using people's names and placing them on the public record whereas if we dealt with these matters in committee it could be done behind closed doors where some of these problems could be threshed out.
In reply to the hon. member's question I have found that the cases are very much the same in provincial courts in my experience. The hon. member wants to know if there is any machinery requiring efforts at reconciliation. In these cases from time to time you will find a man or woman who has encountered marital difficulty because the other party has been unfaithful and yet in a decent desire to preserve the marriage the individual enlists the aid of a minister, social worker, close friend or sometimes a psychiatrist to attempt to get to the bottom of the problem and find out what is wrong but there is no compulsion on people to do so. If people want to disagree they cannot be compelled to agree and live out their lives fighting with each other.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 2 agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, I have one or two brief questions on this bill. I appreciate that it may not be a good practice to place people's names and incidents on the public record but I am more particularly

concerned about the question of the evidence and the surrounding circumstances relating to the acceptance of these by the committees of the other house. My questions will follow the same pattern as before with respect to the acceptability of the evidence and the manner in which it was collected in an effort to ascertain if there appeared to be some organizations or individuals who make their entire livelihood out of appearing as professional witnesses in these cases. Was the evidence in this instance obtained by what we classify as private detectives and, if so, would you indicate who they were?

In this case there was one private detective named Etheridge who appears quite frequently in divorce cases before committees of the other place. There must always be corroborating evidence under the rules of the other house and in this instance the corroborating witness was the husband.

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to say a few words in connection with the civil service and its relationship to members of parliament.
During recent weeks there have been a number of misunderstandings between the civil service and members of parliament, which 1 feel is a great shame because we are dependent on each other to a very great extent, perhaps more than most people realize. I think perhaps the people in the government service do not realize the influence they have on the life of a member of parliament. So far as the public is concerned, every action taken by a member of the government service, every letter written and every decision made, is laid right on the doorstep of the member. A curt letter written on a hot summer day, poor judgment exercised by an official or an inspector, long delays in answering inquiries, an impatient or perhaps supercilious manner of treatment of a member of the public who has a complaint, all fall back on the member concerned who has to take the brunt of any of these indiscretions and the difficulties which may arise as a result thereof.
Members of the government service may not at times realize the importance of their actions to the members concerned. To the public the government is one being; it does not matter whether a cabinet minister, deputy minister, inspector, secretary in the office or a member of parliament is concerned; everything done on behalf of the government is done by one body. That is why I feel that an efficient government service is so very necessary to members of this house.
I would like to carry this thought one step further. Every minister of the crown is responsible for every person in his department; he must be able to rely upon everything done by such people and he must, I believe, feel that those in his department are loyal to him and to the people who have elected him.
I would like to say a word about the criticisms that civil servants have been loafing on the job. Examples of such people can
Supply-Secretary of State no doubt be found in any large organization including the government service-that is inevitable. But in all fairness, I wonder how many of these people who have nothing to do are in this position because they have not been given anything to do. This may be because their immediate superior is away and perhaps much of this mushrooming in the government service over the war years has probably resulted from similar conditions. Until such time as the service gets back to normal 1 have no doubt that there will be many people who have nothing to do but who are nevertheless willing to work.
With respect to the effort made in past years to prevent government servants from becoming politically influenced, this has created an artificial barrier between members of parliament and the government service and I think it has gone too far. It has created too many difficulties and something should be done to remedy this situation. I think it is fair to say that at the moment a good many government employees-and this probably applies in the civil service commission-feel that members of parliament are meddlers who are trying to find positions in the government service for people whom they wish to help for political reasons. In many cases the member of parliament is actually the only person who knows those involved, but this problem has reached the stage where many members of the government service are afraid to be seen talking to a member of parliament unless he happens to be on official government business.
I feel that this whole situation is not political, it is not a question of a member of parliament belonging to one party or another, but it is rather a case of an organizational difficulty brought about by a desire to prevent undue political influence. This method of handling the situation has actually created an even greater difficulty. I think in cases where government employees have occasion to deal with individual members they find us to be fair and reasonable people and on the other hand members have found individual public servants to be sincere and anxious to do a good job. As groups, however, we do find a barrier between us, whereas we should be working together for the good of Canada.
It is, of course, true that the civil service is in a difficult position. Generally speaking, people employed in the government service are professional men and women. They are employees of the crown and they must be loyal to the department by which they are employed and they often find it very difficult to go outside of that department for assistance with respect to their difficulties. It is for this reason that I think it is important that civil

Supply-Secretary of State service organizations and associations should present their difficulties and problems to the government in the very strongest way.

W. Whitehouse indicated the willingness of federation representatives at all times to meet with members of parliament or a select committee to assist in maintaining the efficiency of the public service.

I would urge the government to give consideration to the problems and suggestions I have outlined.

I have a few remarks to make on the qualifications required by the civil service. In this connection I have received a number of representations before and since I have been a member of parliament concerning the difficulties experienced by a number of men in this country with respect to qualifying for the civil service because of what is felt to be a rather narrow restriction under the veterans statutory preference.
Now there is no denial that the men in the armed services who have come back from war should have every opportunity to rehabilitate themselves, and undoubtedly the principle of rehabilitation must be given very serious consideration when we are selecting candidates for the public service of this country. However, one realizes that during this past war there were hundreds and thousands of men who because of no fault of their own since they were instructors or because they were retained for one reason or another did not go beyond the confines of this country. If I am correct in my interpretation of the statutory preference they are in a second category and cannot qualify.
I feel that perhaps the commission in reviewing the civil service framework might now consider enlarging the scope of the statutory preference to include these men, who have a lot of skills which they could offer to the public service of this country. After all, we do not find this restriction imposed by most-I cannot say by all because I may not have all the information-of the provincial and municipal governments. The effort of the men who served in this country was in many instances just as efficacious in prosecuting a victorious campaign during the last war as that of the men who proceeded overseas and I feel they should have an opportunity to serve the public of Canada in the federal civil service. Why there should


be any differentiation between the federal civil service and any provincial civil service I have yet to discover. I offer this as a suggestion. There may be arguments which would indicate that the present policy is the correct one, but I offer this for serious consideration.
In addition, for the past number of years there has been a large number of immigrants to this country, people who have come from the British Isles and other allied countries and who, in many cases, have served along with our service men. Many are professional people of various kinds; they have many skills, and I believe they would be eminently qualified in many cases to serve in the public service of this country but, again, they are excluded, although they are accepted in the civil services of the provinces and of the large municipal governments. I would again suggest that these men who come to this country should have the opportunity to qualify for the federal civil service, and I commend this proposal especially to the commission when considering its recruiting policy.

I should like to say a few words on this question of the civil service before the vote is carried. I begin by referring to some of the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Edmonton West in his suggestion to the minister and to the civil service commission that perhaps the question of veterans preference should be carefully examined in the light of the conditions that have developed since the end of the war.
I recognize, as I am sure do all hon. members, that he has raised a problem which is of some importance. This question of veterans preference with regard to the civil service is, of course, a diminishing one because so many of the positions have age limits attached to them and veterans are getting older. But I certainly hope that in any consideration given to this problem the legitimate interest of veterans and especially of disabled veterans, who certainly deserve every kind of preference they can get, will not be interfered with. Of course, I do not suggest for a moment that the hon. member had such a thing in mind when he spoke.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka had some interesting things to say about the civil service generally. If I venture to follow him and speak on this matter it is not only because of my position in the house but because I had the honour of working in the civil service for 20 years, from 1928 to 1948, in which year I left the civil service, not for the reason indicated by the Prime Minister the other night but for the very opposite reason.

Speaking, then, as a former civil servant I think I can say that the civil service of Canada has gained a reputation second to none among the civil services of any free country in the world for integrity, efficiency and loyalty. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka said that if there is loafing -I think that was the word he used-in the civil service it was due to the fact that insufficient work was being passed on to those particular civil servants affected by this disease. It certainly does not affect any of us in the House of Commons this year. In my own experience of 20 years in the government department over which I later had the honour to preside, we did not suffer at all from the disease of loafing, indeed if there was anything which was wrong with that department it was that the officials were more often overworked than they were underworked.
The hon. member also mentioned the fact that a barrier sometimes develops between members of the public service and members of parliament. That may well be true, and it is not surprising, I think, that there should be a feeling of that kind in the minds of some members of parliament because officials, if they are loyal to their obligations, have to be careful in their relationship toward members of the political service. My own experience in the department over which I once presided-and I think it is an experience which has been shared by other ministers- was that members of the public service must be very careful to help members of parliament in any way they can, irrespective of the party to which those members belong, in respect to the giving of factual information, but there is always a difficulty developing when a member of the public service is asked to express opinions, even privately, or to give information which may go a little beyond the factual. Perhaps I am not the person who should emphasize that possible danger because it should not be one which could cause any harm to any member of parliament on the opposition side. But there is that possibility and because of that I think there always will be a species of official barrier between the civil servant and-if I may call him that-the political servant.
Mr. Chairman, in 1950 I had the honour of speaking to the professional institute of the civil service of Canada and if I may I should like to place on Hansard some of the words I used at that time because they describe exactly the way I feel now. In addressing them I said:
In selecting persons for employment in the service of the Canadian government we have sought-
And I am sure the same situation prevails now-

But however efficient the civil servant may be, however industrious, however underpaid,-	'

-I do not suppose you will ever be able to erase completely from the limited minds of some people the distorted picture of the "bureaucrat" as an indolent person, conceived in influence and born in politics, who fattens at the public trough: and works a couple of hours a day winding and unwinding red tape.

But I have also learned that, at times, there is one thing far more delaying and destructive than red tape; that is misguided and premature efforts to cut across wise and well established administrative rules. You can, I suppose, get more toothpaste more quickly by' squeezing the top of the tube. The result is messy and wasteful.
I said then, and I feel the same now:
I do not, therefore take seriously the recurring joke about the complexities and delays of public administration, and I know that we have every reason in Canada to be proud of our public service.
One reason for which we can show pride in our public service is the loyalty of its members to the government of the day which is the very basis of the existence of a nonpartisan civil service, its obligation of loyalty to the government of the day whatever government may be in power. That means not being loyal to one political party or to a group of persons who may come and go but to the state itself as represented by the government of the day. I am quite sure that Canadian civil servants will recognize that obligation in the future as they have in the past.
The civil service has obligations under the Civil Service Act but it also has rights under that legislation. One of the rights it possesses under that act is the right of independence from political pressure. One of the obligations it has under the act is to give loyal and devoted service to the government in power. It also has the right under the act,
1 believe, to hope for promotion in accordance with merit.
One of my hon. friends to my right raised some questions this afternoon about the promotion policy inside the civil service. I recognize that that is a very important matter in connection with morale which in turn

Supply-Secretary of State is important in terms of efficiency. The hon. gentleman was basing his remarks in part on the observations of Professor John Deutsch who himself was a distinguished civil servant for many years. He thought perhaps promotions were not quick enough for those who were young and gifted and that this might in a sense militate against the hope that all civil servants have for a successful career. Before taking my seat I should like to ask the minister a question. I understand that a rather comprehensive reorganization of the civil service commission is being undertaken at the present time by the chief of the civil service commission who, if I may say so, I am very glad to see on the floor of the house tonight in his third capacity in recent years. I should like to ask the minister if he could give the house some information as to how that reorganization which will be an extremely important one indeed is proceeding and in particular I wish to know whether in that examination consideration is being given to the possibility of separating the foreign service in some respects from the civil service and bringing it under a foreign service act.
When I say that consideration might be given to this I am not thinking, of course, of taking the foreign service out of the civil service in the sense that it should not be maintained as a professional service outside politics. I do not want anything like that to happen to it. Whatever may be its control I think it must remain as non-partisan as is the civil service. However, I happen to know from experience that conditions which govern the operations of the foreign service, especially of those members of it who have to work abroad, are so very different from the conditions which govern work and service in Canada that very often the regulations which are right for a civil servant working at home are not applicable in any


reasonable way to a civil servant working abroad. Therefore this matter which I know has been brought up once or twice in the past is an important one. The question is whether or not we should have a foreign service act governing the operations of the foreign service based on the same principles as the Civil Service Act. Perhaps the minister might have something to say about that when he replies. Meanwhile I shall simply repeat what I said a moment ago that I am very privileged to be on my feet this evening paying my humble tribute to the work of the Canadian civil servant.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to discuss a question which has been a problem in the Department of the Secretary of State for a number of years but before embarking on that I should, in view of the rather curious remarks that have been made by the Leader of the Opposition to the effect that the government of this country represents the state, point out that I have always believed the constitutional position to be that the crown represented the state.
In regard to the hon. member for Edmonton West I may state that I know from my personal experience he has maintained a continuing interest in the welfare of veterans. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that his remarks this evening were fully in keeping with this traditional keen interest in the welfare of the veterans of this country.
The point I wish to raise is one that has been drawn to my attention by labour union officials in my constituency concerning a situation which causes them grave concern particularly in the winter months. They have advised me that some of the civil service personnel and armed forces personnel in Saskatoon have been taking employment in their spare time as painters, carpenters and work in other fields with the result that the regular employees in these trades have lost job opportunities. The union officials have also pointed out, Mr. Chairman, that this practice tends to depress wage rates in the trades affected; they say it has enabled some unscrupulous employers to undercut regular rates of wages and contracts.
These moon-lighters can and do work at less than regular rates of pay. They can do this because they already have jobs for which they are paid out of the public treasury. In some instances, no employer is involved because in some cases the contract is taken up directly by the civil service personnel or the armed forces personnel with the householders to do painting, carpentry work, and so on. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this matter should be looked into in order that ways and means may be found to prevent

regular workers being placed at this disadvantage. In this connection I hope that the experience that the department has had in other years with this problem will not prevent them from taking a new and realistic look at this particular problem that is being raised here.
I certainly agree, Mr. Chairman, that there is a problem of conflict in that it is thought that the government of Canada should not interfere with the private lives of individuals it employs and it is a difficult problem to reconcile those opposing points of view. It is my hope that the Secretary of State will inquire into this matter to see what can be done and also to bring it to the attention of the Minister of National Defence in order that some sort of satisfactory solution can be worked out so that regular employees in those trades will not suffer the disadvantage I have mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I heard the Secretary of State (Mr. Courte-manche) say that he was not responsible for the civil service commission but that he was the spokesman of the house to the civil service commission. I take note of his statement and, if it is true that he is the spokesman of the house to the civil service commission, I am sure that he will ask the officials of this body to kindly take under careful consideration the suggestions made by hon. members.
For years, the Conservative party, as well as the Liberal party, have had nothing but commendation for the civil service commission, its higher as well as its minor officials.
I believe that everyone recognizes that the civil service commission is well administered and that civil servants behave as they should. As it is, by some strange coincidence, no sooner did the Conservative government come into power that certain decisions of the civil service commission were no longer quite in accord with past decisions. In fact, some time ago, I put a question to the Secretary of State concerning applications for employment. The Secretary of State knows about it since I have discussed the matter with him on several occasions. I feel keenly about this problem and I am anxious to see it solved for I feel that this new decision will prevent hundreds, if not thousands of people who would like to work for the civil service commission to put in an application and to take the required examinations, thereby losing a chance to get a job with the civil service commission.

That situation is all the more important as it affects more particularly the electors of the Secretary of State since, according to the reasons he has given for the implementation of that new policy, people living in far away and isolated localities could suffer the most from that change of policy on the part of the civil service commission.
This has to do, as everyone knows, with the applications made for a competition which may be held in 5, 6 or 8 months. The Secretary of State has told us that such applications are returned to candidates who are informed that they are no longer accepted unless a competition is open and that they may learn about the date of the next examination by reading the newspapers or looking up the advertisements posted in public buildings.
Thus, if six or twelve months go by before an examination is held, that means the poor candidate has to buy the newspaper- La Presse, or whatever other newspapers interest him particularly-just to make sure that he does not miss the advertisement when it appears. The hon. Secretary of State surely knows that the civil service examinations are not advertised in the weeklies of Labelle constituency-unless the Secretary of State's influence has penetrated that far. It is only rarely that such advertisements appear in the Echo de la Lievre or the other weeklies so well known to the Secretary of State.
The hon. Secretary of State replied that they stopped publication because there were too many applications, 40 per day; yet, on the other hand, he claims that he wants to improve the standard of the commission's work, and thus to make the personnel more productive. Well, I can hardly think of a more important service to the public than giving them this information, and making it easier for them to compete in all these examinations.
The hon. Secretary of State extricated himself in a vague way by saying that the applications are often of a general nature. But it is not these that are involved- rather it is a question of applications of a specific nature, such as when a candidate applies for work as a postman in the Post Office Department. What is the cost to the civil service commission in terms of work, or services, or literature, or correspondence to file the application and reply to the applicant: "Dear Sir, I have received your application, and you will be notified when the examination is to be held". The civil service commission is well aware that there are slips, all made up in advance which

Supply-Secretary of State are sent to the applicant, and when the examination is held, the candidate receives a notice and has only to report for examination at the place and time mentioned in the notice.
I am wondering therefore why this public service has been eliminated. If it is true that 40 people apply for jobs every day and that those applications are returned, it means that by the end of the year a total of 14,600 will have unsuccessfully applied for a position with the civil service commission, and I say this is an insult and an injustice to these people. What will happen is that when competitions are held, there will not be enough candidates, and it will indeed be difficult to fill all the vacancies because you must not forget that, for the Post Office Department alone, when a competition was held, out of 400 people approximately applying during the year, only about 200 of them succeeded. These people were put on an eligible list; the ones on top of the list were hired first and then the others in order, until the list was exhausted. What is easier, fairer and more logical for the applicants? You take it from me that the next time the Post Office Department holds an examination, there will not be 40 applicants. Indeed, nobody will be aware that a position of clerk is open at the Post Office, and you will have to hold examinations monthly to obtain an adequately sized staff to give the efficient service the public is asking for, the kind of service it is entitled to get from the Civil Service Commission and the Post Office Department.
We are told this is done in order to save the salaries of one or two grade I clerks at $2,000 each or a total of $4,000. But these two employees still cannot be dispensed with, as they will now be busy answering applicants whose requests cannot be accepted. Therefore this will not reduce the expenditures of this department. As a matter of fact these $4,000 will help in all fairness the
14,000	persons who apply for work at the civil service commission; besides, a period of unemployment is hardly the time to reduce the staff.
Has the hon. Secretary of State, like his colleague the hon. Postmaster General, the intention to replace labour by electronic machines? The Secretary of State should not expect two mail deliveries a day, as promised by the Postmaster General when he was in the opposition. You will have only one delivery a day, as in the past, because

the election is also a thing of the past. Moreover, as the riding of Labelle is somewhat far away, the announcement of a competition will arrive one or two days late, because there will be no second mail delivery, whatever the hon. Secretary of State may say.
As to the notices posted in public buildings you hardly imagine, Mr. Chairman, that a would-be applicant living in Ste. Anne du Lac would walk 32 miles every two or three days to the Labelle post-office, in order to see whether there will be a competition, so that he may file his application. With all due respect, I submit that such conditions are nonsensical; this is cheese-paring economy. I will even go further and say that it is not an economy, since you will keep the same personnel. In fact, the number of employees has increased. This is no time to cut down staff, especially to deprive the public of one of the most useful services.
I suggest that any Canadian has a right to seek employment in the civil service, and if an applicant must rely solely on ads published in the newspapers or notices posted in public buildings, it makes no sense. That decision taken by the civil service commission is bad; it is mere cheese-paring economy
What will be the result of such a policy? The hon. Secretary of State will get hundreds of letters from people who want a job in the civil service, and he himself will have to establish files for all those people who wish to become civil servants.
There won't be any lack of candidates, in such a case.

Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that the spokesman for the civil service commission has heard the hon. member for St. Denis speak clearly enough for the commission to know that nobody likes such changes and that a year from now, or with the least possible delay, the commissioners will correct this unfair practice with regard to some fifteen thousand Canadian citizens who want to apply for work at the civil service commission.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few brief words on the subject of age. In this country today, as in most other western countries, we are facing a real social problem in the employment of what might be called middle aged citizens. It is ironic that in an effort to provide greater security at the end of life pensions plans brought into

industry have made it very difficult for persons over 40 to secure employment. I just want to express the hope that when the commission investigates plans for reorganization of employment they will take into account the very serious question of making employment available to more older persons who may have come on the labour market through no reason of inefficiency and the possibility of their applying for employment in the civil service. One applicant came to me who had been turned down on account of age. The employer, he said, wanted someone with a master's degree, 20 years of experience and not over 23 years of age. That is an exaggeration, of course, but the problem does exist. I hope that the commission will take it into account in their planning.

Before the minister answers the hon. member for St. Denis I should like to raise a question having to do with the reply that the minister made to the hon. member on July 2, as found at page 1832 of Hansard. I was particularly interested in the English translation of the last remark made that day by the minister when dealing with the question of the hon. member. The Secretary of State is credited with saying:
It is a commission which was instituted by the former government, and I have to suffer the consequences.
I discovered this a short time ago and it does not seem to jibe with the statement made by the minister this afternoon which I looked at in the Hansard office. I wonder whether he would explain the change which seems to have taken place from the statement of July 2 to the one he made this afternoon.

No, I did not change my mind. I should like to say that if the hon. member for St. Denis has some difficulty I have the same difficulty, but I am not responsible for the difficulty he has. The civil service commission is carrying out its own job and if we have some difficulty I am not responsible and neither is the hon. member for St. Denis. That is the explanation I gave on that date.
(Translation):

May I ask the Secretary of State who is responsible for that situation? He tells us that he is the spokesman for the civil service commission. If he is the spokesman for the civil service commission, and if there is nothing he can do, he should not take it upon himself to present and explain the
Supply-Secretary of State estimates of the civil service commission. Moreover, he says that the civil service commission was instituted by the former government. I believe the Secretary of State makes a slight mistake. The civil service commission was created more than 22 years ago. If the Secretary of State remembers weil, the civil service commission exercised its authority throughout the country when the Conservative government was in power. The answer of the Secretary of State, besides being inaccurate, is far from being gratifying. After all, he says that as it is the work of the former government, we must suffer the consequences. If, for instance, the number of unemployed people has doubled, are we to suffer the consequences? You made the whole election campaign by promising that you would improve the situation. Well, improve it.
The hon. member for St. Denis says 22 years. I shall go further and I tell him that the civil service commission was set up in 1918.
Yes, for Ottawa but not for the nine provinces.

I have never suggested anything else. It was formed in 1918 and the two governments have always respected the authority of the civil service commission. It was purposely made free from political interference and if the day should come when this situation no longer obtains, this to my mind, would be most unfortunate.

Could the Secretary of State obtain from the two officials sitting in front of him the exact date when the commission changed its policy with regard to those examinations? I would also like to know if, before adopting this new attitude, the civil service commission had communicated with the then secretary of state?

I am informed that the commission changed its method of receiving applications about three months ago. Now, if that new procedure proves inefficient, the commissioners will come back to the former method. I am told that the civil service commission receives more than 13,000 applications per month. As a general rule, such applications are classified so as to be kept for later reference. If a competition is open, it is easy for the commission to notify the applicants.

So as to clarify that matter, may I add this: I am not talking about a

Supply-Secretary of State person sending a general application but about a person applying for a particular position in a given department, a position for which that person would be called upon to compete if there was an examination. The Secretary of State has been a private member of parliament and he knows that the Post Office Department hires about a hundred persons in a year. If a competition is advertised for three or four days only in the newspapers, not enough candidates will apply. What will happen is that, instead of having four hundred candidates, you will have about 40 and out of these perhaps as many as 20 or 25 will fail. This means that for the Postmaster General there would be only fifteen qualified applicants and that, in a month's time, new notices would have to be sent out and new examinations held. This is very dangerous in a different way. In fact, when an examination is about to be announced by the commission, civil servants themselves and their relatives are the first to know about it. If this new policy is kept up, in twenty years' time the civil service will be solely a huge family affair, made up of so and so's cousins and his sisters and his aunts, for those would be the only ones to know that a job is open and an examination is to be held.
In my opinion, it would be in the general interest that this decision be reconsidered. The Secretary of State said that he is only spokesman for the commission; consequently, he can admit with me that this decision is a mistake. It is human to make a mistake. It could be that all this was only an experiment. In that case, I think the experiment has already lasted long enough.
I have here seven applications that were returned. I am sure that when a further competition is held those applicants will not be notified or, if the competition is advertised, they will forget to read the papers. You cannot ask these people to scan the newspaper for months on end, so as not to miss their chance to compete for some job. This applies to all hon. members. Everyone of us receives applications that we have to put on file. If we have to do the work of the civil service commission so as to save work for two clerks who, in any case, have to answer the would-be competitors that their applications are declined, it is hardly worth the trouble. In fact, the commission is not saving a cent. Not only does it fail to serve the public, but it is doing an injustice to thousands of people.

A few moments ago, the Secretary of State did not answer the second

part of my question. Did the civil service commission communicate with the Secretary of State before introducing the new procedure?

The answer is no. I can
however tell my hon. friend from St. Denis, after consulting my officials, that they are willing to reconsider the case he mentions and that they will see to the matter.

I congratulate my good friend the hon. member for St. Denis on having raised this matter. In the constituency I have the honour to represent, there are about 12,000 civil servants. In my opinion, this decision of the commission is contrary to its usual good administration. Prior to that, the civil service commission was beyond reproach. I think the increase in the number of applications is mainly due to the great number of unemployed now in Canada. I congratulate the Secretary of State on having consulted his officials and I believe their decision to reconsider this question goes to prove that they are intelligent and willing to try again after having realized they made a mistake.
I admire the Secretary of State who had the courage a moment ago to reaffirm that he will brook no political interference in the civil service. At present, as far as I am concerned and as far as I know-and I believe that I know much about it-we do not, in my opinion, give enough political freedom to civil servants. I am not in favour of having
150,000	employees in the civil service, either in the Department of Public Works or elsewhere, who are all intelligent men or women, and who cannot tell whether they are Conservatives, C.C.F'ers, Liberals or anything else. We live in a democratic country and if we want true democracy, it is not reasonable to prevent our civil servants from freely expressing their political opinions.
Allow me, Mr. Chairman, to give you an example. I have waged five electoral campaigns. Each time, at least 400 or 500 civil servants, from the Department of Public Works or from crown corporations, have spoken against me, against the party and even did organization work for my opponent. I have never denounced any one of them. There was even a civil servant who ran against me on behalf of another political party. He was a very likeable young man and the only thing I told him during the campaign was that, after the election, if he needed my assistance to get his job back, I would be glad to help him.

He came again to me and I made him the same offer.
The sister of one of the candidates, a woman who held a job as clerk grade III at the experimental farm-and a very competent one-campaigned against me for two months. She was holding down her job in the civil service and, in her spare time, she travelled around campaigning on behalf of her brother. After the election, several of my supporters came to me and requested that I report those people so they would lose their jobs. What did I say? I asked them if they themselves would like to lose their farm, their store or their job. They replied that they wouldn't like it. Well, I was surely not going to make them lose their job.
Civil service employees are entitled to their opinions. Naturally, I would not wish a civil servant to cry out on the roofs that he worked for such and such a department and that certain things go on in that department which he could unmask; his audience might believe these statements, even though he might be lying. I admit that civil servants have no right to go that far in politics; but, outside that, I have never caused anybody to lose his job. I have always said that if those were their ideas, they were free to come out in favour of one party or another.
What happened? All those people which my hon. friends wanted me to get discharged voted for me at the next election. I could tell new members that if they think they can make a civil servant lose his job because he did not work for them during the election campaign, they would be doing an injustice to that man. And if they make him lose his job they will lose a hundred votes or more at the next election.
I would therefore advise the ministers not to pay too much attention to the new members. As far as the new members are concerned, may I tell them not to pay too much attention to their organizers who could very easily make them commit very serious mistakes in this regard. Even though I have succeeded in business, I have been active in politics for several years and I will admit that there are some intelligent people among the Conservatives.
They are all intelligent.
If you are among those who are intelligent, that means you are a Liberal.

If they are not bright, we do not keep them.

I will not go on any longer, convinced as I am that you will reach an understanding with the civil service commission so that it may continue, as it has in the past, to announce competitions in the newspapers and to accept applications for employment.
Mr. Chairman, may I say to the Secretary of State that, in his constituency, just as in my own, farmers no longer get their mail at the post office. People in villages no longer go to the post office. They hand the postal box key to one of their children or to someone else who goes and fetches the mail. As people in towns no longer go to the post office, they are not in a position to see the advertisements except in the newspapers. Or they will go to the post office for a couple of months and then they will forget about it and the time limit for the competition will pass, which will cost money and will not give satisfaction.
Now then, I am sure the civil service commission which is made up of as honest and intelligent people as we can wish will see to it that justice is given to everybody.
We live in a democracy and civil servants have the right to believe that they would be better off under the Conservatives than under the Liberals or under the C.C.F. than under the Conservatives or the other way around. And it would be a great injustice to try to prevent one or all civil servants who are just as intelligent as the members of the House of Commons, from expressing their opinion. They should have freedom of thought except in cases of extravagance or in cases where these employees would not do their job in a satisfactory way. In such a case their immediate superiors are capable of dealing with the matter.
I am sure the Secretary of State will take these few remarks in good spirit and that he will be careful not to rely too much on the recommendations of new members, also that those new members will not be too enthusiastic in having those who may have worked against them in the elections dismissed. If too many civil servants are dismissed, Conservatives will all be swept off at the next election.
